mechanism: A compiler lets a person state intent in a high-level language while a toolchain produces correct machine code for a fixed, fully documented target: the instruction set (ISA). Three things made this work. (1) The target was frozen and characterised: IBM 704 and later x86 behaviour was specified exactly, so one translation step was correct for every machine of that kind. (2) Checking was nearly free: you compile, run and test in seconds, so mistakes cost minutes, not scrap. (3) Copying was free: once written, the compiler and every program it produced could be copied at zero cost. FORTRAN (manual Oct 1956, compiler Apr 1957) is credited by historians with cutting the statements needed to program a machine about 20x. Skill moved from "knows the machine" to "knows the problem", so the number of programmers, and of programs, exploded. The deep point: the compiler did not make the knowledge abundant. The frozen target did, by making the compiler's knowledge reusable everywhere.
hardware_analogue: The real analogue is a full stack of compilers: intent/spec -> design compiler (generative CAD/topology, sized to the requirement) -> process compiler (CAM, process plan, toolpaths, heat-treat and inspection plan) -> machine code (G-code, printer/robot instructions) -> evidence compiler (inspection data, certificate of conformance, qualification package). It needs its own "ISA": a characterised, frozen process with published design rules. Hardware has done this once, in semiconductors. Mead-Conway (late 1970s) introduced technology-independent design rules. MOSIS (1981, DARPA) pooled designs onto shared multi-project wafers. Logic synthesis (Synopsys Design Compiler, 1986-87) compiled RTL to gates against a foundry's cell library and PDK. TSMC (1987) sold the frozen target as a service. Result: fabless companies grew from 24% of IC sales in 2010 to about 50% in 2024. Mechanical and energy hardware has no PDK. Every shop, alloy heat, casting house and machine tool is a different, undocumented "ISA".
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical: the target is not deterministic. Material lots, machine wear, fixturing, residual stress and porosity mean the same instructions give different parts. So the correctness of a design depends on a particular line's capability (its Cpk), and that is rarely measured or published. Checking is slow and destructive: a turbine blade or pressure part is proven by fatigue, creep or burst tests that take weeks to months and destroy samples, not by a 2-second run. Legal: in regulated hardware the output must carry evidence, not just geometry. FAA PMA/STC, ASME stamps, NRC 10 CFR 50 Appendix B, MIL specs and DLA source approval all attach to a specific supplier, process and data package. A part that compiles is not a part that is approved, and approval queues run 6-18 months. OEMs hold the design data rights and the qualification history. Economic: low volume per design (thousands, not billions of copies) means nobody pays to characterise a process into a PDK. Every shop treats its process knowledge as a trade secret. Fragmented demand gives no TSMC-scale buyer a reason to freeze a target. Semiconductors escaped only because one process served about 10^9-10^12 identical copies, which paid for characterisation.
what_ai_changes_now:
In 2026 AI collapses the per-design labour at each compiler stage:
- Design: text/spec-to-CAD tools (Adam, YC W25, $4.1M seed; Neocad, EUR 550k, Apr 2026) and surrogate-model optimisation.
- Process: CAM programming that took hours now drafts in minutes. CloudNC CAM Assist is used by 1,000+ shops including Lockheed Martin, with $128M raised by Sep 2026.
- Quoting/DFM: instant quotes are now routine (Xometry marketplace revenue $629.6M in 2025, +30%).
- Reverse compilation: scan, metallurgy and AI turn an obsolete physical part back into a technical data package. Most importantly, the hardware analogue of decompiling is now cheap.
- Evidence drafting: AI can draft inspection plans, FMEAs and qualification reports.

What it does not change:
- The physical target is still non-deterministic. AI cannot reduce creep or fatigue test time, and physics sets that clock.
- Regulators still review per supplier and per data package, on human timescales, and do not accept simulated evidence in place of tests.
- Characterising a line (building the PDK) still takes real parts, real sensors and real time.
- AI levels the compiler for incumbents too: GE, Siemens and Mastercam ship the same copilots.

Net: AI makes the compiler a commodity. The scarce thing becomes the characterised, approved target that the compiler emits to.
where_the_analogy_breaks:
1. Copying is not free. Software output copies at $0. A hardware output costs material, energy and machine-hours every time. The compiler gives you abundant designs, not abundant parts.
2. Checking is slow and costly. Software abundance came from cheap trial and error. Hardware failures are scrap, downtime or deaths, so the compile-test loop stays slow and safety-gated.
3. Correct is a legal status, not just a logical one. A compiler's output is correct when it matches the language spec. A turbine part is correct when an authority accepts the evidence. That status is tied to a named entity and cannot be copied with the file.
4. There is no single ISA. Software converged on a few targets (x86, ARM, the JVM, the browser). Hardware has thousands of process-material-machine combinations, and only someone who owns and characterises a line makes one into a target.
5. Abundance can be unsafe. "Anyone can compile hardware" includes weapons and pressure vessels. Safety controls must sit at the frozen target (the qualified line), which incidentally is also where the moat sits.
6. Long life in the field. Software is patched over the air. Hardware lives 30-50 years, so whoever holds the operating history and the installed base keeps the evidence.
who_captures_value_when_it_works:
History says the leveller (the compiler, the shared wafer) rarely captures the value. The owner of the frozen target does, along with whoever owns the products built on it.
- Software: FORTRAN/IBM compilers were given away to sell IBM machines. GCC and Linux are free. The money went to the owners of the target platform (Intel/x86, Microsoft/Windows API, then AWS, which sells the target as rented capacity) and to owners of applications. Red Hat captured a thin layer, about $3.4B at the IBM acquisition, against AWS's roughly $100B+/yr run rate.
- IBM PC clones: the open design levelled assembly. Intel (the ISA plus the fab) and Microsoft (the OS target) captured the value; Compaq and Dell got thin margins.
- Semiconductors: MOSIS (the leveller) was a nonprofit and stayed small. The owner of the frozen process captured the most: TSMC, 69.9% foundry share and $122.5B in 2025. The toolchain duopoly (Synopsys/Cadence) captured a rich but smaller pool. The fabless product owners captured the largest equity value (Nvidia).
- Mechanical: Xometry, a marketplace and quoting compiler that owns no capacity, has $687M revenue and barely positive adjusted EBITDA ($8.4M in Q4 2025). Protolabs built its own compiler locked to its own mills and presses, and owns the factory and its design rules.

Rule: when the compiler is levelled, value moves to (a) the characterised and approved target, (b) the scarce capacity behind it, and (c) the owned product or asset built through it. It does not stay with the compiler.
first_principle: A compiler only makes a domain abundant once someone freezes and characterises the target it compiles to. The durable value then goes to whoever owns that target (the qualified process plus its evidence and capacity) and the assets built through it, never to the compiler itself. Testable: in every compiled domain, the biggest profit pool should sit with the target owner (x86/Intel, AWS, TSMC) rather than the toolchain (GCC, MOSIS, CAM copilots).
company_shapes: Physical-PDK foundry for regulated energy parts (owns the target). Owns a small, heavily instrumented line (5-axis CNC, metal AM, HIP/heat-treat, CMM/CT) qualified once as a process, the way MIL-PRF-38535 QML qualifies a manufacturing line rather than each microcircuit. Publishes design rules for one parts class: hot-section and balance-of-plant parts for out-of-production gas turbines and pumps. AI compiles customer intent or a scanned legacy part into designs that sit inside the qualified envelope, so each new part inherits the process evidence instead of joining a new 6-18 month queue. This is the way it escapes the gatekeeper law: the regulator or customer reviews the process once. It owns the qualification dossier, the characterised process data (its PDK) and the capacity. It is the TSMC position, not the Xometry position.

Decompiler-to-library for orphaned fleets (owns the library and approvals). AI-driven scan + metallurgy + reverse-engineering turns obsolete parts into owned technical data packages for big orphaned installed bases: the 988 US peaker turbines over 30 years old (45.5 GW), legacy military ground and air platforms, and nuclear plant spares through commercial-grade dedication. Production runs under its own approvals (FAA PMA, then a purchased ODA, or a 10 CFR 50 App B program). The moat is the library plus the approvals tied to its name. Decompiling is the step AI made cheap; approval is what makes the result ownable.

Compiled resurrection fleet (owns the asset, is its own approver). Buys old turbines and engines at about $83-110/kW against $790-1,800/kW new. Uses its own parts compiler (shapes 1 and 2) to keep them running and sells firm power. Because it operates the fleet, it approves its own repairs (owner-operator authority), so the regulator queue applies only at the plant level. The compiler is an internal cost-collapse weapon; the value sits in owned MW, operating history and PPAs.

Process-locked defence production line (owns product and line). A frozen, qualified airframe and propulsion process for attritable drones, loitering munitions and counter-UAS interceptors. AI compiles each mission requirement into a variant that inherits the process qualification, as a new chip inherits a PDK. Sells finished product and holds design rights (Anduril-like ownership, not a tooling vendor). The defence buyer qualifies the line and design family once, and variants ship in weeks. Safety and export control sit at the owned line.

Spec-compiled grid hardware maker (owns the product and capacity). Large power and distribution transformers, switchgear and medium-voltage motors are commodity-in-principle hardware with multi-year lead times caused by engineer-to-order design labour. AI compiles a utility's spec into a design from a characterised, pre-type-tested design family, and an owned automated winding/core line builds it. Type tests are done once per family (IEEE/IEC), so each unit inherits the evidence. It owns the type-test portfolio, the line and the backlog, which turns engineer-to-order into compile-to-order.

why_software_became_abundant:
Software became abundant because of three things together:
1. A frozen, documented target. ISAs, then OS APIs, then cloud APIs meant one compiler's knowledge applied to millions of identical machines.
2. Nearly free checking. Compile-run-test loops of seconds made trial and error the main way people learned.
3. Zero-cost copies of both the toolchain and its output.

Together these turned machine expertise into problem expertise. Programmers multiplied (FORTRAN's roughly 20x cut in statements). Then each later layer (C, Java, the web, cloud) raised the abstraction level against a new frozen target. Abundance followed the targets: every big wave of software abundance came after a new target was standardised (the IBM 360 family, x86/PC, POSIX, HTTP/the browser, AWS APIs), and the owner of each target took the largest rent.

mechanism: Open source and shared libraries made software abundant because three costs went to near zero at once. (1) Copying: a copy of code is the original, bit for bit, at zero marginal cost. (2) Verification: you can check that a reused component works in your context by compiling and running it, in seconds and for free, so trust in a stranger's code can be checked. (3) Coordination: copyright licences (GPL, Apache) plus the internet let improvements flow back and compound, so one fix serves every user. Linux won by being 'good enough plus free plus improvable by anyone'. Proprietary Unix vendors (Sun, HP-UX, AIX, SGI) could not match a shared base that every customer improved. Linux went from a hobby kernel in 1991 to 100% of the TOP500 supercomputers by the November 2017 list (https://www.omgubuntu.co.uk/2017/11/linux-now-powers-100-worlds-top-500-supercomputers/amp). Hoffmann, Nagle and Zhou (HBS, 2024) put the cost of rewriting widely used OSS once at about $4.15B, but its demand-side value at $8.8T: firms would spend about 3.5x more on software without it (https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4693148 ; https://heise.de/-10322643). That gap is the mechanism. Write once, verify cheaply, reuse a billion times, and the value of reuse ends up thousands of times larger than the cost of creation. Concentration is extreme too: 5% of developers create 96% of the value.
hardware_analogue: The naive analogue is open CAD files, open reference designs and open TDPs (technical data packages). That is the wrong layer. In hardware the drawing is a small share of what makes a part valuable. Most of the value is the evidence: proof that this geometry, in this alloy, from this process and supplier, survives this duty cycle, plus the permission that evidence earns (FAA PMA, NRC/10 CFR 21 dedication, DLA source approval, UL/IEEE listing). So the true analogue of an open-source library is a shared, referenceable body of qualification evidence plus a cheap, accepted way to prove equivalence to it. The cleanest precedent is not open hardware but generic drugs. Hatch-Waxman's ANDA lets a generic maker reference the innovator's clinical safety evidence and prove only bioequivalence. The result: generics are 90% of US prescriptions but 12% of spend, about $98B of $798B, saving $467B in 2024 and about $3.4T over ten years (https://accessiblemeds.org/resources/press-releases/generic-and-biosimilar-medicines-save-467-billion-in-2024/embed/ ; https://accessiblemeds.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/AAM-2025-Generic-Biosimilar-Medicines-Savings-Report-WEB.pdf). The aviation version is FAA PMA by 'test and computation' or identicality, where HEICO prices parts at about 70% of OEM list or less (https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf ; https://aircraft-commerce.com/wp-content/uploads/aircraft-commerce-docs/Maintenance/2009/ISSUE67_MTCE_A.pdf). The nuclear version is commercial-grade dedication. The 'Linux of a hardware category' is therefore an abbreviated-equivalence pathway plus a reference library for that category. Precedents where the open design layer did spread: the IBM PC's open architecture, where Compaq shipped 53,000 units for $111M in its first full year, then a US first-year record (https://www.britannica.com/money/Compaq). Open Compute, where Facebook reported $1.2B saved over three years and data centres 38% more efficient and 24% cheaper to build (https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/data-center-chips/facebook-open-compute-has-saved-us-1-2-billion). And RISC-V, with roughly 10B+ cores shipped by SiFive alone and an estimated 10% penetration of chip sales by value in 2024 (https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/meta-qualcomm-risc-v-market-share-25-2/). All three are categories where the buyer could verify the copy cheaply (it boots, it computes), which is the software condition.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical: a copied drawing is not a copied part. The same print from a different foundry, heat treat or powder lot gives different fatigue, creep and inclusion behaviour. Verification costs real time that cannot be compressed: fatigue cycles, creep hours, thermal soak, qualification lots. A copy has a marginal cost (material, machine time), and fixes do not propagate to parts already in the field. Legal: hardware designs are protected weakly by copyright and strongly by patents, trade secrets and contractual data rights. Copyleft has nothing to grip, so improvements do not have to flow back. Data rights are held by OEMs and often were never bought by the government. GAO-06-839 found rights gaps limited sustainment on the C-17, F-22, C-130J, Stryker, M4 and others, and C-17 sub-vendors refused to hand over data (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-06-839-highlights.pdf). GAO-11-469 notes data rights can add up to $1B to a major procurement (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-11-469.pdf). Approvals are tied to a holder and do not transfer with the drawing. Economic: the OEM's margin sits in aftermarket and service, so OEMs rationally withhold TDPs. Liability is per unit and falls on whoever signs the conformity, so no one reuses a stranger's design without redoing the evidence. Without a shared verification mechanism, every adopter pays the full evidence cost again. That is the opposite of software, where the first test also serves as everyone else's test.
what_ai_changes_now: Changes in 2026: AI collapses the per-unit labour of rebuilding the knowledge layer. CT scans, CMM data, legacy drawings, maintenance manuals and failure records can be turned into a TDP and a draft equivalence argument (geometry, material ID from spectroscopy and microstructure, FEA/fatigue predictions, a comparison against the reference). The Air Force's Rapid Sustainment Office anecdote, a reverse-engineered, 3D-printed KC-135 part at about $55 all-in including engineering (https://federalnewsnetwork.com/?p=1997090), points to what AI-assisted reverse engineering does to per-part cost. AI can also write the paperwork for dedication packages, PMA test-and-computation reports and 10 CFR 21 evaluations, and decide which few physical tests matter most (surrogate models, active test selection), cutting how much physical testing each part needs. With thousands of parts handled per engineer instead of tens, a library of 10,000 to 50,000 parts becomes economic for a startup; until now only HEICO-scale firms could afford one. Does not change: regulator queues (FAA 6-18 months, DLA source approval 12-18 months; no regulator yet accepts AI-generated or digital-twin evidence in place of a physical test), physical test durations, OEM ownership of data rights and patents, scarce casting and forging capacity, and per-unit liability. It also levels knowledge for incumbents: OEMs get the same tools. So AI makes the copy and the dossier cheap, but not the permission or the capacity.
where_the_analogy_breaks: (1) Zero marginal cost: software copies are free; hardware copies cost material and machine time, so 'free' never happens. The best case is generic-drug economics: a price collapse to roughly 30-70% of incumbent list, not to zero. (2) Verification: software is verified by running it; hardware is verified by destroying samples over time, and the evidence is specific to a supplier and lot, so a shared library does not carry trust automatically. (3) Compounding: no git pull for parts in the field. Improvements reach only new builds, so the network effects of contribution are weak. (4) Licensing: copyleft relies on copyright, which barely covers functional hardware. An open hardware commons can be taken by an incumbent with no obligation to give back, as Open Compute designs flowed to ODMs. (5) Failure cost: a bug in a turbine blade or reactor valve kills people, so regulators guard the gate, and that gate is the bottleneck AI does not speed up. (6) Concentration: Linux had one maintainer and millions of identical x86 machines. Hardware categories are fragmented into thousands of part numbers with tiny volumes each, so the 'library' is a long tail. That makes the economics HEICO's (many niche approvals), not Linux's (one huge kernel). (7) Abundance in software was demand-unconstrained. Hardware abundance runs into energy, materials and factory capacity, which reuse does not create.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says the commons creates the value, and two kinds of owner capture it. The first is whoever owns the scarce complement the commons runs on. The second is whoever signs for the liability and the certification of the copy. Linux: the commons itself captured almost nothing. Red Hat, which sold certified, supported, liability-backed Linux, sold to IBM for $34B in 2018 (https://www.axios.com/ibm-to-acquire-red-hat-for-34-billion-2502954f-386e-4a8f-a42c-0815b1db5de1.html). AWS, owner of the scarce fleet that runs Linux, earned about $11-12.5B of operating income per quarter in 2025, so a single quarter is about a third of Red Hat's entire sale price (https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/aws-revenue-reaches-293bn-for-q1-2025-up-17-yoy/). IBM PC: the open architecture let Compaq and the clone makers flourish briefly, but Intel (the scarce CPU) and Microsoft (the licensed OS everyone needed) captured the durable rents while IBM lost control. Open Compute: Meta saved $1.2B+ as an operator, and Taiwanese ODMs gained volume at thin margins. Generics: volume went up, but generic spend fell $6.4B since 2019 despite rising volume (AAM, link above). Patients and payers captured the value, and generic makers were squeezed. The exception is HEICO, which owns 11,500+ FAA PMAs and adds 300-500 a year, priced at about 70% of OEM under long-term agreements. The approval is what sits between the knowledge and the customer, and HEICO owns it. Lesson for Dhruv: do not be the open library. Be the owner of the approved equivalent (the Red Hat/HEICO position) or the operator of the scarce fleet the library keeps alive (the AWS/Meta position). Best of all, be both, so the library is a cost advantage nobody else can use.
first_principle: Reuse makes a category abundant only at the layer where a copy can be verified as cheaply as it can be made. In hardware that layer is the equivalence proof, not the drawing. So the value of a hardware commons goes to whoever owns the approved equivalent or the scarce fleet that consumes it, never to whoever publishes the design. Testable: in any hardware category, price falls toward generic levels, about 30-70% of incumbent list, only after an abbreviated equivalence pathway exists (ANDA, PMA identicality or test-and-computation, commercial-grade dedication). The margin then accrues to approval holders and operators, not to the open-design contributors.
company_shapes: Resurrection fleet as the 'AWS of the parts library' (fits the current best idea, 20/25): own and operate 30+-year-old Frame 6B/7EA-class peakers (988 US units, 45.5 GW) bought at roughly $83-110/kW versus $790-1,800/kW new. An AI-built TDP library (CT/CMM-to-CAD, material ID, life prediction) keeps them alive. Sell firm power and capacity. As owner-operator you are your own approver for non-FAA industrial parts, which escapes the regulator-queue law. The library is a private cost advantage; the fleet and the power contracts are the asset. Whether to open the library later is a choice, never the business.

HEICO for nuclear: a commercial-grade dedication house that owns a catalog of dedicated, 10 CFR 21-backed replacement parts for obsolete safety-related and important-to-safety components across about 94 US reactors and the coming restarts and uprates. AI cuts dedication from weeks of engineering per part to hours (critical-characteristic selection, equivalence dossier, test plan). The company owns the dedicated-part catalog, the Appendix B QA program and long-term supply agreements. Utilities already accept the licensee or dedicator signature, so no new regulator review is needed per part. Value sits in the owned approvals, priced at generic discounts to obsolete-OEM quotes.

Generic-maker for a non-aviation heavy-equipment category with no gatekeeper (e.g. grid transformers and switchgear components, mining and rail traction motors, industrial compressors): own an AI-rebuilt, test-backed library of equivalent parts plus your own qualified production cell and UL/IEEE listings. Sell under long-term agreements at about 60-70% of OEM aftermarket list, the HEICO price point in an unregulated category. Defensibility comes from accumulated test history and installed-base agreements; evidence compounds where code cannot.

Contractor-owned legacy defence fleet (adversary air or ISR or target drones, the Draken/Top Aces shape): buy retired airframes cheaply, keep them flying with an AI-reconstructed TDP and parts library, and sell flight hours to DoD and allies. Operating the fleet makes you the approver under your own maintenance programme rather than a DLA source-approval applicant, which escapes the 12-18 month queue, and it monetises the data-rights gap GAO documents rather than asking DoD to fix it.

Red Hat of an open reference design, owning the certified build and installed base: sponsor or adopt an open reference design for a fragmented, supply-constrained category (e.g. modular substations, battery-storage power conversion, or a standard robot actuator). Let the commons drive adoption, but own the only UL- or utility-certified, liability-backed production plus the fleet-leasing and service book, the way Red Hat owned certification and support while the code stayed free. The value is the installed base and its operating evidence.

mechanism: Cloud (AWS, from March 2006) turned a lumpy, upfront, single-tenant purchase (servers, racks, power, ops staff) into metered, per-hour, multi-tenant capacity reached through an API. It rested on four conditions at once: (1) fungibility: one x86 VM is like any other, so any tenant's workload runs on any box; (2) a programmable interface: capacity gets provisioned, configured and torn down in seconds with no human in the loop; (3) statistical multiplexing: thousands of tenants with uncorrelated demand pool onto one fleet, pushing utilization up and unit cost down; (4) near-zero transport and switching cost: bits move at light speed and workloads move between machines with no requalification. With all four in place, the fixed cost of starting (buying hardware before building anything, per Madrona's McIlwain) became a variable cost, and the number of experiments rose by orders of magnitude.
hardware_analogue: The true analogue is not 'Uber for factories' (a marketplace of RFQs). It is a pooled, owned, qualified capacity fleet behind a compiler-like interface. why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical: machines are not fungible. Each part needs fixtures, tooling, toolpaths and setup (hours to days), and the output is atoms that must be shipped. what_ai_changes_now: AI in 2026 attacks fungibility and the interface, which are the two missing cloud preconditions. Concretely: it generates CAM, toolpaths and process plans automatically from CAD, quotes instantly, and designs fixtures, which cuts setup from hours toward minutes. It schedules across mixed machines. It does in-process inspection and sensor logging, so every part carries a machine-generated evidence record (digital traveler), which makes a process, rather than a part, the thing that gets qualified. It reverse-engineers obsolete parts and generates test plans. It handles predictive maintenance that keeps old assets running. Together these let one owned, qualified facility run thousands of part numbers the way one AWS region runs thousands of tenants. What AI does NOT change: regulator queues (FAA, DLA and NRC still take 6-18+ months, and none yet accepts AI review or digital evidence in place of physical tests), the physics of transport, capex per unit of capacity, correlated peak demand, and liability.

mechanism: Software became abundant because checking that a change is safe got cheaper than making the change. A unit test runs for fractions of a cent per minute of CI compute. It runs on a bit-identical copy of the shipped artifact, so a passing test says something about every copy in the field. It can be rerun forever at almost no marginal cost. And the developer, not an outside body, decides whether the result is good enough. Together, determinism, identical copies, near-zero-cost reruns and an internal approver turned verification into a by-product of every commit. Because change was cheap and reversible, teams could ship continuously. Amazon reported a weekday deploy every 11.6 seconds in 2011, with up to 1,079 deploys in an hour. DORA's 2021 report found elite teams deploy 973x more often than low performers, and in 2019 elite change-failure rates were 0-15% versus 46-60% for low performers. Cheap verification also let strangers' code be trusted (open source, package ecosystems, APIs), which is what made software generic, high quality and non-monopolistic. Type systems and test suites are the 'proof that it's safe' kept as code, next to the thing they protect.
hardware_analogue: The real analogue is not 'simulation' in general. It is 'delta qualification': cheaply proving that a changed part, material, process or software build is equivalent to, or no worse than, a baseline that is already accepted. Hardware already has a 'type system'. Design codes and allowables (ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code, MMPDS/NCAMP material allowables, UL standards) are type checkers: stay inside the allowables and the design is 'safe by construction'. The unit-test equivalents are coupon tests, automated rigs and validated simulation. The CI-pipeline equivalent is certification evidence produced automatically as a by-product of every design change. That means requirements traceability, a model run, a physical anchor test and inspection data, bundled as one artifact a gatekeeper will accept. Existing precedents are certification by similarity, nuclear commercial-grade dedication, PMA parts approved by test and computation, and, as of 2026, BMW's virtual crash tests accepted as equivalent for some German homologation tests.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today:
The reasons are physical, legal and economic.

Physical:
- The unit you test is not the unit you ship. Every casting, weld or AM build is a sample from a distribution with variance in material and process, so a test proves the design and the process window, not each unit.
- Many tests destroy the item: a full-scale crash test costs about $500k.
- The worst failure modes play out over long periods and can't be run faster: creep, fatigue, corrosion, irradiation. The Alloy 617 nuclear code case targets 100,000-hour service, and INL noted only five alloys were qualified for elevated-temperature nuclear construction, none of them nickel-base.
- Qualification data can become invalid after even minor changes to the processing route (NASA).

Legal:
- The judge is outside the company (FAA, NRC, UL/NRTLs, DLA, insurers) and carries liability, so it trusts evidence only once it has a history.
- FAA AC 20-115D gives model-based credit only when the same process was 'previously found acceptable by the FAA on a certified project'. That is chicken-and-egg: the newcomer can't get credit for a process until it has used it on a certified project.

Economic:
- Qualifying a new material empirically takes 5-20 years and millions of dollars (NIST, QuesTek, NASA).
- Level A software for planes costs about $25-100 per line, with verification up to 80% of the cost (vendor estimates).
- Those fixed costs can only be recovered over large production volumes, and the evidence is the OEM's proprietary data. So qualification is a moat, not a utility. Test cells, ranges and crash labs are scarce physical capacity.
what_ai_changes_now:
What AI changes in 2026:
- **Faster simulation.** Surrogate and ML models make simulation orders of magnitude faster. Instead of running a few FEA/CFD cases you can sweep thousands of process and geometry variants. BMW and Mistral partnered in June 2026 on AI crash simulation.
- **Paperwork.** AI can generate and maintain the evidence paperwork: requirements traceability, test plans, conformity reports, code-clause mapping, similarity arguments. Per earlier laws, this is per-unit labour, which AI does fix.
- **Per-part inspection.** Computer vision plus in-situ sensors (melt-pool monitoring, CT, ultrasonic) give 100% per-part inspection records instead of sampled ones. This attacks the variance problem directly.
- **Reverse-engineering.** Geometry and material can be recovered from a scan, which feeds 'equivalent to baseline' arguments.
- **Test planning.** Active-learning test design picks the fewest physical anchor tests needed to validate a model. DARPA Open Manufacturing targeted a 40% reduction in AM qualification time.
- **Early signs that gatekeepers are moving.** German authorities accepted BMW's virtual crash tests as equivalent for some homologation tests (Feb 2026). The NRC reportedly finished one licensing type in 9 months versus about 4 years, aided by AI (single secondary source). The 2025 executive order sets an 18-month NRC review target.

What AI does not change:
- Time-dependent physics (100,000-hour creep, fatigue).
- The need for physical anchor tests to validate the models.
- Who carries liability.
- Scarce test capacity.
- The rule that gatekeepers accept a process only after it has a history.

Most regulators still don't review with AI or accept digital-only evidence in their queues.
where_the_analogy_breaks:
1. **Software tests cover identical copies; hardware is a population.** Passing a test on one artifact never certifies the next unit, so the hardware 'test suite' must include per-unit inspection and process control forever. The cost of verification never goes to zero, only to the cost of anchor tests plus inspection.
2. **There is no rollback.** A failed turbine disk, pressure vessel or airframe is irreversible and can kill people. Tolerance for a change failure rate is about 0%, not the 0-15% elite software teams achieve. So hardware will never deploy every 11.6 seconds. The realistic win is going from years per qualification to weeks, not from days to seconds.
3. **The judge is outside the company.** In software the developer is the approver. In hardware a third party with liability is, so cheap verification only creates abundance where the owner is allowed to judge its own evidence.
4. **Models degrade outside their validated range.** A surrogate model that is right inside its training data can be confidently wrong outside it. That is the opposite of a type checker, which is sound by construction.
5. **Tests don't stay valid on their own.** Code with a fixed hash stays tested. Hardware ages, so evidence must be refreshed with operating data.
who_captures_value_when_it_works:
History says the tool that makes checking cheap rarely captures the value; the owner of the evidence that judges accept does.

**Software:**
- Test frameworks (JUnit, pytest) captured roughly zero; they are free.
- CI vendors captured modest value. Travis and CircleCI faded; GitHub sold to Microsoft for $7.5B, mainly for its repository and network, not CI.
- The big winners were operators who used cheap verification to change their own owned systems faster than rivals. Amazon's deploy cadence led to AWS.

**Hardware differs.** The checking tools DID capture value, because a validated simulator carries decades of accepted-evidence history and is itself the trusted judge:
- Synopsys paid $35B for Ansys (closed July 17, 2025).
- Certifiers that own the mark capture rent: UL Solutions had about $3.1B revenue in 2025, a 17% operating margin and a market cap of roughly $15-19B.

The pattern: value goes to (a) whoever owns the trusted judge or mark (approval, accredited lab, validated model with test history, allowables database), and (b) vertical operators who are their own approver and use fast checking to keep changing an asset base they own. SpaceX test-fires Raptors dozens of times a month at McGregor; the airlines that hold their own engineering approvals are another case. It does not go to whoever sells the simulation or AI-paperwork tool to incumbents, because AI levels that knowledge for incumbents too. An AI 'CI for hardware' SaaS fails the project rules. Owning the approved evidence plus the assets it unlocks passes them.
first_principle: A physical industry turns generic and abundant exactly where the cost and time of proving a change safe, in a form the gatekeeper accepts, falls below the cost of making the change. The value goes to whoever owns that accepted evidence and the assets it unlocks, not to whoever sells the checking tool. Test: measure the ratio of time-to-acceptance to time-to-design-change in a sector. Where AI plus anchor tests drives it below about 1 (power-gen parts, ground vehicles, PMA parts), copies and second sources should multiply within 5 years. Where it stays above 10 (new nuclear alloys, new aircraft types), incumbents keep their monopoly.

why_software_became_abundant:
Verification became nearly free, deterministic and self-administered:
- Every copy is bit-identical, so one passing test speaks for every copy.
- Reruns cost fractions of a cent.
- The developer is the approver.
- Mistakes can be rolled back in minutes.

So the cost of trusting a change, including a change from a stranger, fell below the cost of making it. That made continuous change possible (Amazon: a deploy every 11.6 s; DORA elite: 973x the deploy frequency of low performers) and made it safe to compose open-source parts written by strangers. Abundance came less from cheaper writing of code than from cheaper trust in code.

mechanism: Zero marginal cost of copying and distribution. Software has a large fixed cost to write the first copy and almost no cost for each copy after that: a bit-identical copy needs no qualification, and the network delivers it. This made software abundant for three reasons. (1) Each copy is guaranteed to be identical, so a test of one copy is a test of all of them, and the evidence comes free with every copy. (2) No one has to give permission per copy: since 1976 the copy and the right to run it have been the same thing, and open source licences (GPL 1989) took the permission layer away altogether. (3) Distribution became cheap because of the internet and app stores, and computing became cheap because AWS sold it by the hour from 2006. Startup capital needed fell from millions of dollars to thousands. The result: Linux runs about 96% of the top 1M web servers (https://w3techs.com/technologies/segmentation/os-linux/web_server) and about 83% of EC2 instances (secondary source: https://electroiq.com/?p=14452).
hardware_analogue: The real analogue is not the 3D printer. It is a qualified design file whose physical copies inherit the evidence of the first copy. That needs three pieces together. (a) Digital inventory: a validated technical data package, which the Navy calls a 'manufacturing recipe', stored in place of stock on a shelf (https://all3dp.com/4/from-lab-to-fleet-will-the-navys-2025-3d-printing-wins-trigger-acceleration-in-2026/). (b) Process control tight enough that 'qualified once, printed anywhere' holds for a family of parts. (c) Standard modules made in volume, so the fixed cost of design and qualification is spread over many units, and Wright's law gives roughly 20% lower cost per doubling of cumulative output. Solar modules fell 99.6%, from $106/W to $0.38/W between 1976 and 2019 (https://ourworldindata.org/learning-curve). Li-ion packs fell to $115/kWh in 2024, down 20% in one year (https://about.bnef.com/blog/lithium-ion-battery-pack-prices-see-largest-drop-since-2017-falling-to-115-per-kilowatt-hour-bloombergnef/). Design reuse across a fleet is how hardware gets closest to 'one build serves billions'. GE's LEAP fuel nozzle tip took a part of more than 20 brazed pieces down to one printed design, 25% lighter and five times as durable, and about 100,000 have been printed in Auburn, AL (https://www.ge.com/news/reports/epiphany-disruption-ge-additive-chief-explains-3d-printing-will-upend-manufacturing ; https://manufactur3dmag.com/ge-aviation-produced-its-100000th-3d-printed-fuel-nozzle-tip/).

why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical: atoms are not bit-identical. A copy's properties depend on the powder lot, the machine, its thermal history and post-processing, so a test of one unit is not a test of the next. Every new site, machine or material means requalification. Copying the geometry is free; the copy's material state is what costs money. Legal: in hardware, permission is attached to each unit and each source, not given once. That covers FAA PMA and TC/STC, NAVSUP/DLA source approval (12-18 months), nuclear 10 CFR 50 Appendix B / commercial-grade dedication, and OEM data rights in TDPs (see the Army tire valve case). The design file may be copyable, but the right to install a copy is not. Economic: (1) the OEM's profit is the aftermarket, so it has every reason to keep data closed: PMA prices sit 30-50% below OEM, and OIG found 2-80x markups. (2) Demand is long-tail. A fleet needs thousands of different parts at volumes of 1-100 a year, so Wright's law never gets enough doublings on any one SKU. (3) Delivery still needs logistics and installation labour, and outage time costs far more than the part.
what_ai_changes_now: 2026, what changes: (1) Building the first copy gets cheap. AI plus CT or 3D scanning plus legacy drawings can rebuild a TDP from a worn part, including inferred material, tolerances and a draft FEA. That turns reverse-engineering an orphan part from weeks of engineer time into days, and the cost of each digital-inventory SKU falls from tens of thousands of dollars to thousands. This is what makes the long tail economic to digitise. (2) Process-signature ML (melt-pool monitoring, in-situ CT, a digital twin of each build) makes 'qualified once, printed anywhere' plausible for a family of parts. The evidence becomes a data stream per build rather than a destructive test per lot. That is the closest hardware gets to software's free test. (3) The paperwork of a qualification package can be drafted automatically: cert matrices, CGD dedication plans, PMA test plans, NSN substitution packages. (4) Generative design merges many parts into a few standard modules (GE nozzle, 20 to 1), which shrinks the SKU count and concentrates volume on fewer SKUs, so Wright's law has more to work with. What does NOT change: regulators still review on their own human timelines and do not yet accept AI-generated or digital-twin evidence in place of physical tests. Data-rights law does not change. Bad castings, powder supply, and the fact that a failed part on a turbine or aircraft has a life-safety cost all stay. AI also lowers the cost of first copies for OEMs and HEICO, so knowledge alone gives no moat.
where_the_analogy_breaks: (1) Copies are not identical. Every hardware copy carries its own risk, so a 'qualified copy' always costs something per unit (inspection, traceability, liability). It never reaches zero, only goes down. (2) There is no network to distribute through. A printer near the point of use still needs feedstock, a qualified operator, post-processing, NDT and installation; at best it replaces a shipment, and the field work stays. (3) Failures are physical and correlated. A bad file copied to 1,000 turbines is a fleet-wide grounding, not a patch, so regulators make copying slower on purpose. (4) Demand is the reverse of software's. Software is one SKU with billions of users; fleet hardware is thousands of SKUs with tens of users each. Zero marginal cost helps standard modules (solar, cells), while digital inventory helps the long tail. These are two different businesses, and only standard modules get Wright's law at scale. (5) Hardware does not cut out the middle layer the way the internet did. The holder of the approval stays between the file and the asset. (6) Software abundance destroyed price, while hardware abundance moves price to whatever is scarce next: energy, uptime, capacity. That is where an owner can win.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says the party that levels the field rarely captures the value. What gets captured is the scarce complement next to the free copy. Software: Linux was free; Red Hat captured about $34B by selling certified, supported copies, that is, the evidence and permission layer; AWS captured more by owning the scarce physical layer (data centres) and selling usage. IBM PC: the architecture was cloned; Intel (the scarce fab) and Microsoft (the licensed OS on the installed base) captured the value, while IBM and the clone makers did not. Hardware precedents: solar's 99.6% learning curve was captured mostly by Chinese makers with scale capacity and by owners of utility-scale assets and PPAs, not by the inventors; the GE nozzle's value stayed with GE because GE holds the TC and the LEAP installed base; HEICO captures PMA value because it owns approvals, not printers. Printer makers (Stratasys, 3D Systems, Desktop Metal) and 'digital warehouse' platforms are the levellers, and most have destroyed value. So when copying a design becomes cheap, value goes to (a) whoever holds the qualification or approval for the copy, (b) whoever owns the installed base or fleet that uses the copies and sells its output (power, uptime), and (c) whoever owns scarce physical capacity (qualified print/HIP/cast lines, fabs). The play under the project rules is to be (a) and (b) together: own the fleet, own the qualified library, and be your own approver.
first_principle: When AI and digital manufacturing make copying a hardware design nearly free, value does not go to the file or the copier. It goes to whoever owns the evidence and permission that a copy is safe to install, plus the installed base that uses the copies. This is testable: across qualified-part markets, the price premium over commodity cost should track the cost and wait of qualification (PMA 30-50%, DoD 2-80x), not the cost of manufacture.
why_software_became_abundant: Three conditions held together, and all three must hold. (1) Free copies: each copy cost near $0 and was bit-identical, so testing one copy tested them all. (2) Free permission: one licence covered everything, and later open source removed the licence entirely, so no gatekeeper reviewed each copy. (3) Free distribution and compute: the internet and app stores made reach global at no marginal cost, and AWS (2006) turned capital spending into a pay-per-hour cost, so a $5k team could ship to a billion users. The fixed cost was spread over enormous volume, so the cost per user went to near zero, and abundance followed: Linux on about 96% of top web servers.

mechanism: Interfaces, APIs and protocols (TCP/IP, POSIX, USB, the IBM PC BIOS/ISA bus) froze the contract between components so either side could be replaced without the other's permission. Three properties made that work in software. (1) Copying a contract was nearly free: Compaq clean-room re-implemented IBM's BIOS from the spec in roughly 9-12 months for about $1M and sold $111-150M in year one. (2) Proving conformance was nearly free: if the code compiles and passes a test suite, it conforms, and you can check that in seconds as many times as you like. (3) Breaking the contract was costly to the incumbent: once the installed base depended on the interface, the owner could not change it without stranding its own customers. The result is plug-compatible competition. Each layer becomes a commodity, the number of suppliers per layer explodes, and prices fall toward marginal cost. Abundance came from decoupling: an improvement in one component no longer needed the consent or redesign of the whole system.
hardware_analogue: The real analogue is not 'standard bolts'. It is form-fit-function (FFF) equivalence plus a qualification record that lets a buyer swap one physical part for another without asking the OEM. Hardware already has examples with numbers. The ISO shipping container cut port loading costs from $5.86/ton (break-bulk, 1956) to about $0.16/ton. FAA PMA parts are third-party FFF replacements for OEM aircraft parts, priced 25-65% below OEM, in a market of about $11.8B (2025). Nuclear commercial-grade dedication (10 CFR 21) turns a commercial part into a safety-related one by proving its critical characteristics. The Open Compute Project published server and rack interfaces: Facebook reported 24% lower build cost and 38% less energy, with PUE of 1.07 against 1.5. DoD's MOSA (10 USC 4401) mandates modular open interfaces for major programs started after 2019. In modular plants, skids, containerised power and standard substation modules play the role of plug-in components. The hardware 'API' therefore has three layers. The geometric and electrical interface (easy). The behavioural contract: materials, tolerances, fatigue, thermal and failure modes (hard). The permission to substitute: approval, warranty and insurance acceptance (the real chokepoint).
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical: a hardware interface is never fully specified. Two parts can fit identically and still differ in creep life, metallurgy, coatings and vibration modes. Conformance can only be shown statistically, by destructive tests, rig hours and operating history, and that costs about $50k-$1M+ and 6-24 months per part number. Software conformance is close to free. Legal: OEMs own drawings and data rights. They tie warranties, long-term service agreements and insurance to genuine parts. Regulators (FAA PMA 6-18 months, DLA source approval 12-18 months, NRC Part 21) approve each part and each applicant, so every substitute pays the permission cost again. Economic: demand per part number has a long tail. A gas turbine or weapon system has 10^4-10^5 part numbers, most sold in single or double digits a year, so the fixed cost of reverse engineering plus qualification per part exceeds the revenue per part. Only the top few percent of high-volume parts ever get a second source (HEICO's model). OEMs know this. They price the long tail at monopoly margins and change interfaces at each model update. Incumbents also have a reason not to standardise: the aftermarket is where the profit is. HEICO's Flight Support Group earns 24.1% operating margins on approved substitutes alone.
what_ai_changes_now: In 2026 AI collapses the per-part-number fixed cost of building the behavioural contract. Scan-to-CAD (a turbine blade scanned in about 5 minutes at 0.01 mm), automated drawing and tolerance inference, and ML material and coating identification from samples all apply here. Surrogate physics (FEA/CFD/fatigue) can rank which characteristics are truly critical. LLM agents can assemble the qualification dossier: dedication plans, PMA test-and-computation packages, similarity analyses and Part 21 paperwork. Fleet sensor data can be mined as operating evidence. Engineering per part plausibly falls from about $50-200k to about $5-20k. That moves the break-even from the top 2-5% of part numbers to perhaps the top 30-50%: the long tail opens up. AI also makes the reverse direction cheap. It can write an open FFF interface spec for an entire legacy fleet, which is a de-facto 'API' that no OEM published. What AI does NOT change: the regulator's queue and its demand for physical tests; fatigue and creep life, which still need cycles or service hours; OEM data rights and warranty voiding; insurer acceptance; and foundry or casting capacity for single-crystal or large forgings. AI levels the knowledge for incumbents too. GE and Siemens can also cut their own aftermarket engineering costs.
where_the_analogy_breaks: 1) Software conformance is binary and free to check. Hardware conformance is probabilistic and expensive, so the 'interface' includes evidence that builds slowly over time. 2) A copied software component costs nothing to reproduce. A hardware substitute still needs atoms, tooling, castings and inventory, so it never falls to zero marginal cost: abundance means 'many suppliers at 30-60% lower prices', not free. 3) A software failure is usually recoverable. A hardware failure can kill people and creates liability, so the permission layer is legitimate and cannot be engineered away. Safety controls are the price of entry. 4) Network effects: TCP/IP won because every new node raised the value for everyone. Most physical interfaces have weak network effects outside logistics (the container) and data centres (OCP), so no one has a natural reason to push a standard. Standards in hardware are usually imposed by a dominant buyer (Facebook for OCP, DoD for MOSA, US/ISO for containers), not grown bottom-up. 5) The installed base locks in an old interface for 30-50 years. That is bad for new standards but good for whoever makes the old interface open, because the fleet already exists.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History is consistent: the leveller rarely keeps the value. It goes to whoever owns the scarce complement that remains after the interface becomes a commodity. In PCs, Compaq and Phoenix (the clone BIOS) levelled IBM, but Intel (the CPU) and Microsoft (the OS), the non-commoditised chokepoints, captured the profit pool, and IBM lost the market it had created. In Linux, the kernel was free. Red Hat captured certified support and sold to IBM for $34B on about $3B revenue. AWS, which operated Linux as a fleet, captured far more: about $107.6B revenue and about $39.8B operating income in 2024. In containers, McLean's Sea-Land was eventually sold off. The value went to scale carriers and ports (Maersk, terminal operators) and to shippers and consumers. In aviation PMA, the value goes to the holder of the approvals library, HEICO, at a 24% margin, not to the airlines that ask for second sources. In OCP, hyperscalers (the operators) captured the savings, and ODMs got thin margins. The rule: value goes to whoever (a) owns the permission or evidence that makes a substitute legal and trusted, or (b) operates the fleet that turns cheap commodity components into a premium output (compute, firm power, flight hours). It does not go to whoever publishes or reverse-engineers the interface.
first_principle: When AI makes a hardware interface cheap to copy, the value moves to whoever owns the right to substitute (the approvals and evidence library) or the fleet that turns cheap substitutes into a premium output. Test: in every case where an interface opened up (PC, Linux, containers, PMA, OCP), the profit pool should go to the holder of the permission or the operator, not to the leveller.

why_software_became_abundant: Interfaces made components substitutable, and substitutability made each layer competitive. A copied interface costs near zero, conformance tests run in seconds and can be repeated forever, there is no physical marginal cost, and network effects pushed everyone onto one protocol. Each time an interface froze, supplier count rose, prices fell toward marginal cost, and innovation moved to the layer above. Abundance did not come from cheaper knowledge as such. It came from cheap, permissionless proof that a substitute works.

mechanism: Package managers (CPAN 1995, Maven Central, npm 2010, PyPI, Cargo) made any component available on demand from one global registry. Four things had to be true together. (1) A machine-readable interface contract: a name plus a semantic version range lets a solver prove that version B can stand in for A. (2) Copying costs nothing, so supply is unlimited and no one competes for a unit. (3) Trust is checked after the fact: you install first, and if something breaks you patch it and roll back the lockfile within minutes. (4) A lockfile records the exact resolved graph, so any build can be reproduced. Together these turned "find, judge and integrate someone else's work" from weeks of negotiation into one line. Scale: npm holds about 3.1 to 3.3M packages (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Npm). Sonatype estimated 6.6 trillion open-source downloads in 2024, 4.5 trillion of them from npm, up 70% year on year (https://www.sonatype.com/press-releases/sonatypes-10th-annual-state-of-the-software-supply-chain-report). The registry is not where the value sits. The resolver's proof of equivalence plus free copying is what does the work.
why_software_became_abundant: In software, reuse cost fell from a licence negotiation plus integration work (weeks, tens of thousands of dollars) to zero dollars and seconds. Once reuse is nearly free, every new product is about 80-90% assembled dependencies, so a small team can ship what used to need a large company. Abundance came from the fact that substitution can be decided by computation. A version constraint is a cheap proof that A can replace B. Because nothing is used up, a popular package never runs out, and because rollback is cheap, a bad package costs little. Each of these three properties is missing in hardware, and this is what the analogy depends on.
hardware_analogue: The true analogue is not a parts catalog. Catalogs already exist at software scale: DigiKey lists more than 16.5M products and added over 1M in 2024 (https://www.eenewseurope.com/fr/digikey-enrichit-son-catalogue-avec-plus-de-32-000-nouveaux-produits-en-stock-au-deuxieme-trimestre-2025/). McMaster-Carr stocks 700k+ items and 98% ship the same day (https://www.mcmaster.com/international). Octopart searches the whole electronics market and had 20M users in 2024 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octopart). The analogue that matters is a resolver for certified equivalence: given part A in application X (its loads, temperatures, vibration, regulatory class), prove that part B, made by supplier S, is a legal and safe drop-in, and record that proof as an artifact others can reuse (a "hardware lockfile"). Such proofs already exist, in fragments and held by whoever controls each approval: FAA PMA approvals, nuclear commercial-grade dedication packages under 10 CFR 21, DLA QPL/QML listings, and utility approved-vendor lists. A PMA is the purest case: an approved substitution for an OEM part. HEICO holds 11,500+ of them and adds 300-500 a year (https://www.ramapo.edu/rfg/wp-content/uploads/sites/370/2022/06/Heico-Pitch.pdf), and sells them 30-50% below OEM price (https://scuttleblurb.substack.com/p/heia-heico-corp-niches-get-riches).
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical reason: a part does not have a semantic version. Whether it is equivalent depends on how it is used (fatigue, thermal coupling, material lot, process drift), so A=B holds only inside one application envelope. Proving it takes destructive tests, operating hours and teardown, which cost real dollars per part number, often $50k-$1M+ and 6-18 months. Example: a QPL evaluation of samples and the site inspection is forecast to take up to 8 months per manufacturer, at the applicant's expense (https://www.bidnetdirect.com/public/supplier/solicitations/statewide/2620992812/abstract). Supply is rivalrous: a registry can show a part exists but cannot create capacity. In 2021 average chip lead times hit a record 21.7 weeks (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-09-22/the-chip-crunch-grows-worse-as-wait-times-hit-record-21-weeks). Legal reason: liability belongs to whoever signs the equivalence, so the type-certificate holder or OEM controls who may substitute, and data rights to drawings sit with the OEM. Economic reason: OEMs earn most of their margin on aftermarket parts, so they actively oppose second sources. When legitimate substitution is missing, buyers go to grey markets. Known counterfeit incidents in the DoD supply chain rose from about 3,300 in 2005 to over 8,000 in 2008, and the SIA puts counterfeit losses at $7.5B a year (https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/download/2011/11/08/ralph-denino-testimony-110811). Obsolescence (DMSMS) costs the US military hundreds of millions of dollars a year (https://www.navsea.navy.mil/Portals/103/Documents/NSWC_Crane/SD-18/PDFs/Resources/ResourcesDMSMS.pdf). Researchers have found a statistical link between obsolescence and counterfeit reports (https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/a-study-of-correlation-between-dmsms-obsolescence-and-counterfeit/). Put simply, hardware has the catalog but no resolver, and no lockfile you can trust.
what_ai_changes_now: What changes in 2026 is the cost of producing the evidence for each part. AI can now (a) reverse-engineer a part from 3D scans, CT and metallurgy, and write the drawing, material spec and critical characteristics; (b) extract application envelopes from OEM manuals, service bulletins and failure records, so equivalence can be argued for each use instead of in general; (c) draft PMA test-and-computation packages, commercial-grade dedication critical-characteristic analyses and DMSMS form-fit-function trade studies in days instead of months of engineer time; (d) run physics surrogates that narrow a test matrix to the fewest physical tests that will convince an approver; (e) match millions of SKUs across catalogs to find candidate substitutes, as Octopart and SiliconExpert do but extended to mechanical and power parts. Net effect: building one equivalence package plausibly gets 5-10x cheaper, so it pays to dedicate long-tail part numbers that were never worth it before. What does not change: regulator queues (FAA 6-18 months, DLA 12-18 months), the need for real physical test articles and operating hours, rivalrous capacity, OEM data rights, and the fact that the party signing still carries the liability. AI makes producing evidence cheap. It does not make approval cheap. The way through is to be the party that accepts the evidence yourself.
where_the_analogy_breaks: 1) No free copying: every resolved part must still be made, so the registry does not create abundance. Only the right to substitute becomes abundant. 2) No cheap rollback: a bad dependency in software is a patch, while a bad turbine blade or relay is a forced outage or an accident. Trust has to be checked up front, which brings back the gatekeeper. 3) Equivalence depends on context: one npm version works everywhere, but a PMA part is approved for specific engines. The proof covers a graph of applications, not a single node. 4) Supply can be cornered: one stocked-out line card or one casting foundry can block the whole graph, which software never sees except in rare left-pad-style unpublishing. 5) Liability has to sit with someone, so a decentralized, unsigned free-for-all like npm cannot exist. Somebody has to sign. 6) Open source rested on volunteer labour and free copying. Hardware has no Linux-style commons because testing costs money and ships no product.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History is consistent on this: the registry and catalog captures little, while whoever owns the signed equivalences, or the fleet they plug into, captures most. Lesson: own the signed equivalence and the part it lets you sell, or own the scarce piece that stays unsubstitutable. Never own only the index.

mechanism: Software-defined function plus over-the-air (OTA) updates. In software, what a product does sits in code that its maker can change after the sale, at close to zero cost per unit, across the whole installed base at once, and roll back if it goes wrong. This made software abundant for four reasons. (1) Shipping stopped being the finish line: Amazon was deploying to production every 11.6 seconds on average by 2011, and its deploys caused outages about 0.001% of the time. (2) Copying and distributing an improvement cost nothing, so one engineer's fix reached millions of units. (3) Rollback made mistakes cheap, so iteration got fast and the learning loop shrank from years to hours. (4) The asset grew in value after the sale, which made recurring revenue from the installed base possible: subscriptions, unlocks, app stores. The hidden condition for all four is that one party holds 'update authority'. That means it controls the update channel, is allowed to change the asset, and answers for the result. Microsoft (Windows Update), Apple (iOS, App Store) and AWS (it runs the servers it patches) each hold all three.
hardware_analogue:
The real analogue is not 'putting chips in machines'. It is moving the performance of an installed physical asset (how much it can deliver, how efficiently it runs, how long it lasts, what it is capable of) out of the metal and into a control layer that can be changed after the sale. Then the same change is shipped across a fleet. Examples:
- Gas turbines: control-system retrofits (Mark IV/V to Mark VIe or Emerson Ovation, 'AutoTune' combustion tuning) that change output, ramp rate, emissions envelope and inspection intervals.
- Wind turbines: GE PowerUp changed pitch, torque and speed set-points to add up to 5% output. E.ON measured +4% annual energy production on 469 GE 1.5-77 turbines.
- Vehicles: Tesla's 2018 OTA anti-lock braking update cut 60-0 mph stopping distance by almost 20 ft from 152 ft, and Consumer Reports switched to a recommendation. FSD reached about 1.1M paid subscriptions by end-2025 at $99/month.
- Robots and machine tools: new controllers fitted to old arms.
- Grid assets: batteries, inverters, dynamic line ratings.
In hardware the equivalent of 'the code' is the control law plus the operating envelope the asset is permitted to run inside. Usually the envelope is where the money is. Each 1% of output or efficiency on an asset already built is capacity you get without new steel. GE's own example: a 1% gain across 9,000 US 1.5-77 turbines adds more than 420,000 MWh a year.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today:
Physical reasons:
- Most of the installed base was built analog or closed. Many units have no sensors, actuators or compute for an update to act on, so a controls retrofit is a field job. For a GE 6B, a full control-system replacement takes about 25 days of outage.
- Every unit has drifted differently (wear, repairs, site conditions), so one update does not fit every machine the way one binary fits every PC.
- The physical margin bounds the gain. Software can only move a machine inside the limits of its metal. Past those limits you need hardware (GE's Advanced Gas Path claims up to 5% heat-rate gain, but it is hot-gas-path hardware, not code).

Legal reasons. Update authority is split between parties:
- The OEM holds the code-signing keys, the source and the warranty. Deere kept its full repair software dealer-only until FTC v. Deere (filed Jan 2025) was settled with a 10-year order to give the same tools to farmers and independent repairers.
- A regulator must approve changes that affect safety. UNECE R156 requires a certified Software Update Management System for vehicle type approval. A nuclear safety-related digital upgrade needs an NRC license amendment: FPL's Turkey Point RPS/ESFAS replacement LAR was filed in July 2022 and supplemented in February 2023.
- The operator carries the consequences. Nobody holds all three.

Economic reasons:
- The OEM earns more from selling parts and service on old hardware than from making it better. GE Vernova services backlog is about $86-88.5B on an installed base of more than 7,000 gas turbines, over 60% of total backlog. An OEM has no reason to software-extend a unit it would rather replace or service.
- A failed physical update can mean a broken blade or a crash, and the operator's liability is uncapped. Asset owners reasonably refuse updates they cannot validate.
- Fleets are fragmented across owners, so the zero-marginal-cost spreading that made software rich does not kick in.
what_ai_changes_now:
What changes in 2026:
- Writing control code for an orphaned or closed platform is now cheap. That covers reverse-engineering legacy logic, translating Mark IV/V ladder or relay logic into new controller code, and building retrofit kits for discontinued units. This used to be scarce specialist labour, and it is exactly the per-unit labour AI collapses.
- Each machine can get its own model of itself. ML trained on SCADA and historian data can tune each unit separately (combustion tuning, pitch and torque, braking), so heterogeneity stops being the blocker: you learn N set-point files instead of shipping one binary.
- Evidence comes cheaply as a by-product. Before/after measurement, anomaly detection and digital-twin replay make each update's benefit and safety case measurable automatically, and a fleet owner can use that evidence internally right away.
- Validation in simulation is cheaper: closed-loop testing against learned plant models before touching metal.
- Generic, good-quality retrofit controllers become possible for anyone with fleet data, not only the OEM.

What does not change:
- Gatekeeper queues. NRC LARs, FAA STCs and UNECE type approval still run on human review over years. No regulator yet accepts AI-generated evidence instead of tests.
- The physical margin. You cannot code your way past creep, fatigue or metallurgy.
- Outage windows and field labour for the first install.
- Keys and IP. Signed firmware and data-rights claims remain unless an FTC-style order or ownership of the asset opens them.
- Liability. Someone still has to stand behind the change.
- Incumbents get the same AI. OEMs will ship better AutoTune too. Knowledge levels out; update authority does not.
where_the_analogy_breaks:
(1) Rollback is not free. A bad software push reboots. A bad turbine push can crack a combustor, trip a grid, or kill people. Boeing's MCAS was software given authority over physical control surfaces; two crashes killed 346 people. Even in pure software, OTA at scale creates correlated failure: CrowdStrike's July 2024 update downed about 8.5M Windows devices, cost the Fortune 500 about $5.4B (Parametrix), and cost Delta $350-500M. Correlated failure in a power fleet is a blackout.
(2) Marginal cost per unit is not zero. The bits are free, but each unit needs sensors, a retrofit outage, commissioning and its own validation.
(3) Physical capacity caps the upside. Software moves a machine within its envelope, typically +2-5% output or efficiency, or more ramp capability and longer life. It does not create new hardware performance indefinitely the way software features stack.
(4) Writing the code is not where value sits. VW's Cariad lost about €2.4B in 2023 and about €2B in 9M 2024 building its own software stack, then VW paid Rivian up to $5.8B for a working one. Code was abundant; a working, integrated, permitted stack on a fleet was scarce.
(5) Heterogeneity means hardware 'updates' are closer to per-unit tuning than mass distribution. Network effects come from fleet data, not from installs.
(6) The regulator is part of the release pipeline, so 'continuous deployment' becomes 'continuous deployment inside a pre-approved envelope'.
who_captures_value_when_it_works:
History says the code writer does not capture the value. The holder of update authority over the installed base does: whoever owns the channel, the permission and the outcome.
- Software: Linux was the leveller. Red Hat captured some value by selling certified, supported releases, which amounts to selling update authority. AWS captured the most because it operates the machines it patches and sells the outcome (compute). Microsoft and Apple captured value through owning the update/app channel and the 30% store toll, not through writing better code than others. IBM PC clones levelled hardware; Intel and Microsoft captured value as the components every update and install went through.
- Hardware so far: Tesla captures FSD and unlock revenue (about 1.1M subscriptions) because it owns the vehicle stack, the keys and the regulatory filings. GE captured PowerUp through outcome-based sharing on its own installed base. Deere tried to capture repair through software locks until the FTC forced it open, which shows regulators will strip update authority that is held only by locks. VW (Cariad) spent billions writing code and captured nothing. Independent control retrofitters (Emerson Ovation on GE 6B) win projects but get one-time service fees; the asset owner keeps the 5% uplift.
- Conclusion: the party that both owns the asset and controls its update channel captures the value. For a startup under these rules that means owning the fleet: buying assets cheaply because their update authority has been orphaned (out of OEM support, analog, discontinued), installing its own control layer as owner-operator, and selling the output. The software uplift becomes asset value and the startup holds it.
