why_software_became_abundant:
Abundance came from four economics working together:
- Near-zero marginal cost to copy and distribute an improvement.
- Near-zero cost of reversing a mistake (rollback), which made very fast iteration rational. Amazon deployed every 11.6 seconds by 2011.
- A product that gains value after the sale, which turned one-time sales into recurring revenue from the installed base.
- A single holder of update authority: the vendor or operator controls the channel, needs no third party's permission to ship, and takes the outcome.
With deploy cost, error cost and permission cost all close to zero, the learning loop compressed from product generations (years) to hours, and software ate every function that could be put into code. Standard interfaces (x86, POSIX, TCP/IP, then cloud APIs) made those updates portable across heterogeneous machines.

mechanism: In software, every deployed copy reports back. Telemetry and logs are almost free, a rollout can go to 1% of users, and an experiment can be rolled back in seconds. Learning comes from data you collect yourself while operating, not from approval by someone outside. The cost of a learning cycle falls toward zero, so the number of cycles explodes. DORA's 2021 report found elite teams deploy about 1,460 times a year against 1.5 for low performers, roughly 973 times as often. Booking.com runs more than 1,000 A/B tests at once (about 25,000 a year by secondary accounts). Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Facebook each run more than 10,000 controlled experiments a year. Three conditions make this work: (1) the producer owns the running instance (SaaS), so it owns the data; (2) a failed experiment costs little and can be undone; (3) the evidence is judged by the producer itself, through its own metric and its own ship/no-ship call. Software became abundant because quality stopped being decided before release by an outside party. It is now proven after release, inside the company, at near-zero cost.
hardware_analogue:
The true analogue is not "IoT sensors". It is turning operating hours into admissible evidence, owned by whoever runs the fleet. This has already happened in a few places:
(a) ETOPS. FAA Appendix K lets an airframe-engine pair earn long overwater approval from service experience: 250,000 world-fleet engine-hours and an in-flight-shutdown rate of 0.05, 0.02 or 0.01 per 1,000 engine-hours for 120, 180 or more than 180 minutes. Fleet data literally is the certificate.
(b) NRC TSTF-425 and NEI 04-10. Reactor licensees can move most surveillance test intervals into a program they control themselves, justified by PRA and operating experience. The operator becomes its own approver of test frequency.
(c) Waymo and Swiss Re. 25.3M autonomous miles produced 9 property-damage claims and 2 bodily-injury claims, against 78 and 26 expected from human drivers. That is an 88% and 92% reduction, measured on a 200B-mile, 500k-claim baseline. A reinsurer accepted fleet telemetry as underwriting evidence.
(d) Rolls-Royce TotalCare, "power by the hour". Engine health monitoring plus the OEM taking time-on-wing risk turns telemetry into a priced contract.
(e) FDA CDRH documented 73 device authorizations in FY2020-25 that used real-world data. That includes 9 PMAs and 12 PMA supplements, after 90 examples in FY2012-19.
So the hardware A/B test is a fleet-level reliability case: many identical instrumented units, comparable configurations, and a statistically defensible failure rate that a regulator, insurer or buyer takes in place of a new lab qualification.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today:
Physical reasons. Sample sizes are tiny and failures are rare: a fleet has hundreds of turbines, not 100M users. You cannot A/B test a blade crack, because a failed experiment is a fire, an outage or a death, and it cannot be rolled back. Units are not identical either: they differ in configuration, age, duty cycle and maintenance history, so confounding is severe. Statistical power comes slowly, in engine-hours rather than in minutes.

Legal reasons. Regulators prescribe test methods in advance. Accepting field data is the exception, and it is slow (ETOPS needs 250k hours; the NRC needs PRA adequacy under RG 1.200). Liability makes operators hide failure data rather than share it. Data rights sit in OEM service agreements, so the owner often cannot see its own machine's telemetry.

Economic reasons. The one who collects the data is usually not the one who bears the risk. Operators collect it, OEMs monetize it through long-term service agreements, insurers price blind, and nobody holds all three positions. That is why tool sellers failed. GE spent about $4B on Predix and struggled. PowerUp promised up to 5% more output, E.ON measured 4% on 469 turbines, and GE could not capture it as platform revenue. Tesla shows that data alone does not make underwriting profitable: Tesla Insurance's 2023 loss ratio was 92.5% before overhead.
what_ai_changes_now:
What AI changes in 2026:
(1) Cheap sensing plus foundation models for time series and vibration mean condition can be inferred from sparse, messy, legacy SCADA/DCS data and retrofit sensors. Old fleets become instrumentable without OEM cooperation.
(2) Physics-informed models and digital twins can pool evidence across non-identical units. That attacks the small-n problem, so a fleet of 40 heterogeneous turbines can support a defensible statistical life case.
(3) LLMs cut the cost of evidence packaging, which is per-unit paperwork: maintenance-log digitization, failure-mode reports, PRA updates, insurer submissions, commercial-grade dedication packages. This is the "AI fixes paperwork" law working in our favor.
(4) Simulation-plus-field calibration makes counterfactuals possible ("what if we had extended this interval"), which approximates A/B testing on assets where you cannot randomize.
(5) Anomaly detection gives earlier warning, which turns rare catastrophic failures into common, cheap "near-miss" events. That increases the number of learning events per operating hour.

What AI does not change:
- It does not shorten gatekeeper queues. ETOPS still needs hours, the NRC still reviews, and the FAA does not accept AI-generated evidence.
- It does not create operating hours. Calendar time and exposure are still required.
- It does not grant data rights or install sensors on assets you do not control.
- Incumbent OEMs get the same models, and they have more installed-base data.
where_the_analogy_breaks:
(1) No rollback. Software experiments are reversible and hardware failures are not, so hardware learning must lean on predict-then-confirm, not randomize-and-see.
(2) Exposure is time-bound. Users generate millions of events a day; machines generate statistically meaningful failures over years. AI can raise the information extracted per hour but cannot compress the hours.
(3) The judge is external. Software teams judge their own metrics; in hardware, the evidence counts only when a third party (FAA, NRC, insurer, utility interconnect, ISO capacity market) accepts it. The surviving shape is to choose markets where you, or your captive insurer, are the judge: non-FAA industrial assets, merchant power, private fleets.
(4) Heterogeneity. Every physical unit is a fork, so evidence transfers imperfectly across serial numbers.
(5) Incentives invert. Failure disclosure in software is a free postmortem culture; in hardware it is discoverable liability evidence.
(6) Network effects are weaker. A failure dataset improves with scale but saturates. The 10,001st turbine teaches less than the 10,001st user, so the moat is the risk-priced contract built on the data, not the data alone.
who_captures_value_when_it_works:
Experimentation software did not capture most of the A/B-testing value. Optimizely and Datadog are real businesses, but the money went to the operators who owned the instances and the traffic (Google, Amazon, Booking). In hardware, history is the same: the tool makers lost and the risk-bearing owners won.
- GE Predix and Uptake sold the platform and stalled (about $4B spent, and GE later split up).
- Rolls-Royce and GE Aerospace captured the value of engine monitoring by bundling it with risk-bearing service contracts (power by the hour) on an installed base. Secondary estimates put services at roughly 50-60% of Rolls-Royce revenue; that figure is unverified.
- Waymo captures value because its miles feed its own insurance cost and its permit case. Swiss Re gains a better actuarial table, but the operator owns the asset.
- HSB/Munich Re captured IoT value as the insurer: it reported about 506% ROI for its top 10 sensor clients in 2021 from avoided losses, and 13B+ readings since 2016.
- Tesla Insurance shows data without discipline does not capture value (92.5% loss ratio).
Rule: value goes to whoever owns three things at once: the asset, the data, and the risk.
first_principle: In hardware, an operating hour is only worth something if it becomes evidence that someone will price, so the value of a fleet's data goes to whoever owns the asset, the telemetry and the risk all at once. Test: across any hardware sector, operators who bear the failure risk (power-by-the-hour OEMs, insurers, self-operators like Waymo) should earn higher margins on monitoring than those who sell monitoring tools (Predix, Uptake).

Buy 30+-year-old Frame 6B/7EA peakers at about $83-110/kW against $790-1,800/kW new, retrofit sensors, and use AI models pooled across the fleet to build an ETOPS-style reliability case per part and per AI-reverse-engineered replacement component. Sell firm power and capacity. The moat is a growing fleet-hours dataset plus a qualified parts library that no single utility owner has. Because these are non-FAA industrial assets, the owner is the approver, which escapes the gatekeeper-queue law.

2. Fleet owner with a captive insurer, selling availability (power by the hour for the grid). Own a fleet of aging grid assets (gas turbines, large transformers, BESS) and write the warranty and breakdown cover through a captive or a fronted MGA. Fleet telemetry becomes a proprietary actuarial table. Revenue comes from availability contracts and underwriting margin, which copies HSB's loss-avoidance economics but with the owner holding the asset as well as the policy.

3. Autonomous machine operator whose miles are the moat. Own and operate a fleet of autonomous yard tractors, mining-free industrial haulers or perimeter-security robots on private sites, and sell output (moves, patrol-hours) rather than robots. Every operating hour feeds a Swiss-Re-style loss study that cuts insurance cost and supports permits, so the evidence compounds against new entrants. This is the Waymo shape in sectors with private-site, low-regulator exposure.

4. Defence attritable-systems lessor with flight-hour evidence. Own a fleet of low-cost drones or loitering airframes leased by the hour to the DoD and allies. Instrument every sortie and turn the fleet's IFSD-style reliability record into airworthiness and qualification evidence for derivative variants. The company owns the airframes, the data rights (written into the lease) and the qualification history, rather than selling units into a 12-18 month DLA queue.

5. Life-extension owner for one critical, under-instrumented asset class. Examples: big power transformers (multi-year lead times) or reciprocating compressors. Buy them, condition-monitor them, and re-qualify them by fleet-statistical evidence. Lease them back or sell the extended-life output, owning the remaining-useful-life model that utilities and insurers come to accept as the standard.

mechanism: SaaS and recurring revenue: the vendor keeps ownership of the asset (code plus the servers it runs on) and sells usage or outcomes by the month. What made software abundant was not the billing model. Two things sat underneath it. (1) Multi-tenancy at near-zero marginal cost: one shared fleet serves millions of buyers, so capacity is bought in small slices instead of large lumps. (2) The vendor runs the asset, so it sees every unit's telemetry, fixes problems once for everyone, and so cuts both the variance and the cost of operating. Together these moved the buyer from a capex purchase to an opex subscription and moved operating risk onto the party best placed to carry it. The headline result was AWS (launched 2006). VCs and Amazon's CTO said the cost of starting an internet company fell about 100x, from roughly $5M in 2000 to roughly $50k by around 2009-2011. Adobe went all-subscription in Nov 2011, accepted a dip (net income $833M in 2011 to $268M in 2014), and came out with about 70% recurring revenue by FY2015 and $10.46B of Creative Cloud revenue in FY2022. Subscription billing turned unpredictable licence sales into predictable cash flow, and predictable cash flow can be valued and financed cheaply.
hardware_analogue: The true analogue is not "rent the box". It is "the operator owns a fleet and sells the output (kWh, MW-months, tonnes of steam, flight hours, engine-hours, compute-hours), with a guaranteed level of performance". The precedents are Rolls-Royce Power-by-the-Hour/TotalCare (about 60% of the Trent fleet under TotalCare in the early 2000s; services about 53% of group revenue in 2017), GE Vernova long-term service agreements (more than 70% have over 10 years left, about 70% renewal, services more than 80% of Power backlog on an RPO basis), Hilti Fleet Management (first contract 1999, about 3M tools under contract by 2021), and residential solar PPAs and leases (72% of 1.2 GW of US residential solar in 2014 was third-party owned). The step that made solar-as-a-service scale was securitization, not the subscription itself. SolarCity's first solar ABS (Nov 2013, $54M, BBB+) priced at 4.8%, about half the cost of capital then backing distributed PV. In hardware, recurring revenue is a financing technology. The subscription is only the wrapper.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical reasons. There is no multi-tenancy: a turbine, transformer or engine serves one site at a time. Capex is 60-90% of lifetime cost, so selling output means the operator carries the whole balance sheet. Every unit wears out differently, so availability and maintenance cost have fat tails. Moving a failed unit costs a truck roll or a crane, not a redeploy. Legal reasons. Selling output often makes you a regulated entity: utility and third-party-ownership rules for electricity sales, interconnection queues, FAA or military airworthiness approval for flight hours. Approvals and data rights (OEM manuals, part numbers, service bulletins) stay with the OEM, so a third-party operator cannot repair its own fleet cheaply. Economic reasons. Without operating history, lenders price the cash flows as venture risk (10-15%+) instead of infrastructure (5-7%). That gap decides whether selling output beats selling the box. Residual value after 15-25 years is unknowable. And the business is levered and sensitive to interest rates: SolarCity entered the 2016 Tesla deal (about $2.6B) with cash down to $146M and analysts projecting about $2.8B of combined 2016 burn. In software the vendor's risk was a server bill. In hardware it is a ten-year leveraged bet on uptime.
what_ai_changes_now: AI changes three things (2026). (1) Variance. Fleet-wide telemetry plus learned failure models turn unit-by-unit fat-tailed maintenance cost into a predictable fleet number, the same thing multi-tenancy did for software operating cost. Lower variance means a tighter debt spread, and that is the whole game. (2) Per-unit knowledge labour. AI can reverse-engineer and build a parts library from scans, inspection reports and old drawings, plan repairs, and dispatch remote operations. It replaces the OEM's monopoly on knowing how to keep a unit alive, though not the OEM's approvals. (3) Underwriting paperwork. Automated data rooms, performance attestation and investor reporting cut the fixed cost per deal, so smaller fleets can be securitized. AI does not change: interconnection and permitting queues (DLA 12-18 months, FAA 6-18 months, utility interconnection measured in years), regulators' refusal to accept digital evidence in place of physical tests, the base risk-free rate, lead times for metal, castings and transformers, the fact that lenders want about 24-36 months of real operating history before pricing at infrastructure rates, or residual-value shocks from technology or policy change.
where_the_analogy_breaks: (1) Marginal cost. Software's extra unit is close to free. Hardware's extra unit is another full asset, so 'subscription' adds leverage instead of removing it. (2) No pooling of a single asset across customers, so utilization is set by one customer's load, not by statistics across millions of users. (3) You cannot ship a fix to every unit at once; truck rolls and spares inventory scale linearly. (4) Churn runs the other way. SaaS churn is cheap for the buyer; hardware-as-a-service contracts are 10-25 year take-or-pay deals, closer to project finance than to SaaS. (5) Subscriptions did not make software abundant on their own; shared capacity at falling unit cost did. Hardware-as-a-service makes output abundant only when the underlying asset is cheap, as with old turbines at about $83-110/kW against $790-1,800/kW new, or when cheap capital is unlocked. (6) Regulators gate who may sell output (electricity, flight hours) in a way that has no equivalent for cloud software.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says the leveller does not capture the value; the owner of the shared fleet, the cheapest capital, and the operating data does. Software: Linux and open source levelled knowledge, Red Hat captured a slice, and AWS, which owns the fleet, captured the most ($107.6B of 2024 revenue, $39.8B operating income, about 37% margin). Adobe captured value by switching to subscriptions only because it already owned the installed base. Hardware: in aero engines the lessors and airlines took thin margins, while Rolls-Royce and GE, holding approvals, parts and the fleet data, took the aftermarket (more than half of revenue). In solar, panel makers were commoditized and SolarCity, the installer-financier, was squeezed by its cost of capital. Tax-equity investors and ABS buyers earned steady returns, and the operators who survived, such as Sunrun, owned the contract book and the servicing. So value goes to whoever simultaneously (a) owns the units, (b) controls maintenance approvals and parts supply (is its own approver), and (c) has the longest clean performance record, because (c) sets the cost of capital. AI's knowledge levelling lowers (b)'s cost for everyone, OEMs included, so the lasting moat is the fleet plus the operating-history dataset that lowers your cost of debt, not the AI itself.
first_principle: Selling hardware output instead of boxes turns a hardware company into a financing company, so whoever makes fleet cash flows most predictable wins, because predictability sets borrowing cost. Testably: an operator whose AI-driven telemetry and parts library cuts the variance of unit availability and maintenance cost should be able to borrow against that fleet at a measurably lower spread (for example, 300-500 bp below peers after 24-36 months of history) and so undercut new-build hardware sold at a capex price.

Steam-and-heat utility for industry. AI schedules charging against power prices and predicts maintenance, which narrows the variance of output cost. The company owns the assets, the contracts and the thermal-dispatch data, the same playbook as solar PPAs but for industrial heat (about 20% of US final energy use).

Engine-hours green-time fleet. Buy end-of-life CFM56/V2500 engines and life-limited parts, own an FAA Part 145 repair station (bought, not applied for, to avoid the approvals queue), use AI to optimize module swaps and repair approvals, and sell engine flight hours to airlines and MROs at below the OEM's Power-by-the-Hour rates. The company owns the engines, the repair-station certificate and the per-serial-number history.

Contractor-owned ISR and drone-hours for defence. Own a fleet of attritable uncrewed aircraft or sensor nodes and sell surveillance or effect hours to DoD and allies on a contractor-owned, contractor-operated basis; Insitu sold ScanEagle ISR this way. Selling hours avoids per-airframe procurement approvals. AI handles autonomy, fleet maintenance prediction and mission-data processing. The company owns the fleet, the operating record and the security clearances, which are the gating permission.

why_software_became_abundant: Software became abundant because shared, multi-tenant capacity drove the marginal cost of serving another customer close to zero. The vendor running the asset then pooled operating risk and telemetry across all users, and subscriptions turned that into predictable cash flow that markets valued at high multiples. Buyers no longer needed capex or in-house expertise; they bought slices of a fleet. AWS cut startup fixed cost about 100x (about $5M to about $50k), so the number of experiments exploded. The leveller (open source, cheap cloud) made the knowledge free; the fleet owner (AWS) earned the rent.

mechanism: ABUNDANT BUILDERS. Software went from a priesthood to a mass trade because each rung of the craft got turned into something you could copy, at close to zero marginal cost: hardware (cheap PCs, then cloud), knowledge (books, Stack Overflow, bootcamps), reusable building blocks (open-source libraries) and, now, judgement (AI coding). Evidence that the builder pool grew a lot: SlashData counts about 31M developers in Q1 2022 and about 47M in early 2025, +50% in 3 years (https://slashdata.co/post/global-developer-population-trends-2025-how-many-developers-are-there). Evans Data put it at about 19M around 2013 (https://www.fierce-network.com/developer/evans-data-mobile-developers-now-number-8-7-million-worldwide). AI pushes this further, but unevenly. In GitHub's RCT, developers with Copilot finished a task 55% faster (1h11m vs 2h41m; 95% CI 21-89%) (https://github.blog/2023-09-07-research-quantifying-github-copilots-impact-on-developer-productivity-and-happiness/). In METR's 2025 RCT, experienced developers in mature repositories were 19% SLOWER, while believing they were 20% faster (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jul/12/ai-open-source-productivity/). Brynjolfsson/Li/Raymond found AI raised productivity 14% on average and 34% for novices, with little effect on experts, because it 'disseminates the best practices of more able workers' (https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161). The lesson: AI levels the novice up to the median expert by copying the experts' tacit knowledge. It does not make the expert superhuman. What made software abundant was not smarter people. It was that a mistake cost almost nothing (recompile, roll back), so millions of mediocre builders could learn by iterating at about $0 per try, and a cheap shared runtime (the PC, then the cloud) accepted anyone's output.
hardware_analogue: The true analogue is not 'AI makes everyone a welder'. It is the Mead-Conway/MOSIS/TSMC split, repeated across heavy industry. In 1978-79 Mead and Conway took chip design, then 'the sole territory of specialists at large, private semiconductor firms', and made it teachable. Within about 4 years, roughly 110-120 universities were teaching it (https://computerhistory.org/blog/in-memoriam-lynn-conway-1938-2024/). Students sent design files over ARPANET to a shared fab service, which became MOSIS and created the 'fabless design + silicon foundry' paradigm (https://ai.eecs.umich.edu/people/conway/Impact/Impact.html). Design became abundant because a trusted, qualified manufacturing cell took standardised design rules from anyone. The hardware analogue of 'abundant builders' therefore has two halves. (1) AI captures tacit craft: welding parameters, machinist setups, foundry gating and risering, reactor-operator judgement, turbine-overhaul know-how. That collapses training time and lets 5-person teams design hard things. (2) A small number of AI-native, qualified physical cells (foundries, forges, machining and welding cells, test stands) run like TSMC. They accept those designs against published 'design rules' and stamp the output with code compliance. Hadrian already shows half (1) in production: its goal is to get new hires running 5-axis mills in 60-90 days rather than the multi-year apprenticeship (https://jobs.lever.co/hadrian/8ef79201-2683-4d46-831d-2887407e9ebb). Path Robotics raised a $100M Series D (Oct 2024) for AI welding aimed at a projected gap of about 400,000 welders (https://seedtable.com/companies/path-robotics/funding-rounds/series-d-2024-10). Ford is the older precedent for codifying craft into process: chassis labour fell from about 12h8m to 93 minutes by 1914, and the Model T price from $850 to $260 (https://detroithistorical.org/learn/encyclopedia-of-detroit/model-t).
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: PHYSICAL: each try costs real material and machine time. A wrong weld, casting or reactor manoeuvre is scrap, injury or an outage, not a recompile, so nobody can learn by iterating cheaply. Tacit craft lives in hands, eyes and ears (the sound of the arc, the colour of the pour) and was never written down. Capacity is scarce and lumpy: aerospace castings and forgings take about 6-18+ months to make (https://www.bcg.com/publications/2024/fixing-aerospaces-supply-chain-for-casting-and-forging), and per DoD testimony only one US foundry can pour certain large titanium defence castings (https://www.uscc.gov/sites/default/files/2022-05/James_Brown_Testimony.pdf). LEGAL: output is only trusted with a stamp: an ASME Section IX welder qualification and procedure record (WPS/PQR), NADCAP, AS9100, FAA PMA, NRC Part 55 operator licences. Senior reactor operators need about a year as a licensed RO plus simulator and on-the-job phases and an NRC exam (https://careers.jsginc.com/jb/Senior-Reactor-Operator-SRO-in-training-Jobs-in-Lusby-MD/14018438). Each stamp is tied to a person or a site, not to knowledge, so it cannot be copied the way a library can. ECONOMIC: the workforce is ageing out faster than training can replace it. Deloitte/MI estimate up to 3.8M manufacturing jobs needed by 2033, with about 1.9M at risk of going unfilled (https://www2.deloitte.com/us/en/pages/about-deloitte/articles/press-releases/us-manufacturing-could-need-new-employees-by-2033.html). When experienced people leave, quality collapses: Spirit AeroSystems lost many of its most experienced mechanics and auditors, and 787 join-gap defects halted deliveries for about 19 months at a $6.5B cost to Boeing (https://tech.slashdot.org/story/24/01/13/1841233/wsj-boeings-fuselage-factory-plagued-by-production-problems-and-quality-lapses ; https://www.aviationpros.com/aircraft/news/53074175/struggling-with-defects-boeing-supplier-spirit-aerosystems-fires-ceo). There is also no 'PC' for heavy hardware: no cheap shared runtime that accepts anyone's design, except in electronics, where JLCPCB-style $2-for-5-boards prototyping did create abundant hobbyist hardware builders (https://www.brex.com/tools/charge-finder/jlcpcb).
what_ai_changes_now: 2026, WHAT CHANGES: (a) Multimodal models plus cheap sensors (arc audio, thermal and weld-pool cameras, spindle load, vibration) can record a master craftsman's process as data and replay it as live coaching or as robot motion. That is the 34%-novice-lift mechanism moved into physical work: Hadrian's 60-90 day 5-axis ramp, and Path's autonomous welding. (b) AI process engineering (simulating casting solidification, toolpaths, weld distortion) cuts the scrap cost of each try, which brings back some of software's cheap iteration. (c) Paperwork in the quality system (WPS/PQR drafting, traceability packages, first-article inspection reports, commercial-grade dedication packages, operator procedures) becomes close to zero marginal cost. (d) Small teams can design hard things: the 'Mead-Conway textbook' for metal becomes an AI design-rule checker trained on a qualified cell's own yield data. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE (the laws): no regulator or code body accepts AI evidence instead of a physical coupon test, a qualification run or an operating hour. The gatekeeper queues stay (FAA 6-18 months, DLA 12-18 months, NRC). A welder's or operator's licence stays attached to a person. Furnaces, presses, forges and test stands stay scarce and take years to build. AI raises the floor of craft for incumbents as well, so knowledge alone gives nobody a moat. Experts may gain little (METR's -19%), so the lift comes from turning novices into the median expert, not from turning experts into superhumans.
where_the_analogy_breaks: 1) Zero marginal cost: software copies itself for free, but every hardware unit costs material, energy and machine-hours. Abundant designers do not produce abundant parts unless capacity scales too, so capacity, not knowledge, becomes the bottleneck. 2) Cost of failure: a bug ships and gets patched; a bad pressure-boundary weld or a mishandled reactor transient kills people. Hardware needs a stamp from a trusted body ('controlling for safety', as Dhruv puts it), and that stamp is the moat. Software never needed one. 3) Learning loop: software builders learn from millions of free compile cycles. Hardware learning data belongs to whoever runs the physical cell, so the AI's craft improves only for the owner of the furnace or the fleet. Data from operations, not open-source code, compounds. 4) Distribution: the internet delivered software to anyone instantly; hardware needs logistics, installation and service, and installed-base service agreements lock customers in. 5) Open source: a GitHub-style commons for qualified processes cannot exist, because a PQR is valid only for the qualifying organisation. Codes such as ASME Section IX do not let a qualification travel between companies the way a library does. 6) Demand shape: software demand was elastic and new (apps for everything). Most heavy-hardware demand (power, defence, grid) is already there and short of supply, so abundant builders raise output and lower cost rather than creating whole new categories.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says whoever owned the scarce runtime or stamp that all the abundant builders had to pass through captured the value, not the leveller and not the builders. PCs: IBM opened the architecture, and its share fell from about 63% (1984) to about 38% (1987). It lost $5B in 1992 and sold the PC business to Lenovo in 2006. Microsoft and Intel, the chokepoints every clone had to use, took the profits (https://dfarq.homeip.net/why-ibm-left-the-pc-business-in-2006/ ; https://www.csmonitor.com/1987/0406/fibm.html). Open source: Linux made server software free. Red Hat sold the trust and support layer and IBM bought it for $34B in 2019, but AWS, which owned the scarce physical runtime, made $45.6B operating income on $128.7B revenue in 2025, a 35% margin (https://www.nasdaq.com/press-release/amazoncom-announces-fourth-quarter-results-2026-02-05). Chips: Mead-Conway levelled design and created thousands of fabless designers, and the qualified foundry captured the value: TSMC holds about 70% of the foundry market with a 59.9% gross margin on about $122B of 2025 revenue (https://marklapedus.substack.com/p/tsmc-gains-foundry-share-but-others-lose-ground ; https://www.precedenceresearch.com/insights/global-semiconductor-manufacturing-companies). Cars: Ford captured the value of codified craft only because it also owned the plant. So the AI craft-capture tool vendor, the analogue of the bootcamp or Copilot, will mostly be commoditised. Value goes to (1) the owner of the qualified physical cell and its approvals (the TSMC/AWS position), (2) the owner of the operating fleet whose evidence and data compound (the AWS position), and (3) the owner of the scarce installed base (the Intel/Microsoft position). The craft-capture AI should be the company's internal compiler, not its product.
first_principle: When AI makes the craft of building abundant, value moves to whoever owns the scarce qualified capacity, meaning the stamp plus the machine plus the operating data that turns many builders' designs into trusted physical output. So own the qualified cell or the fleet, never the craft tool. Test: in any sector, if craft-AI tool vendors' margins compress while qualified-capacity owners' margins and lead times hold or rise as builder headcount grows, the law holds.
company_shapes: THE METAL FOUNDRY ('TSMC for heavy parts'): an AI-native casting, forging and machining cell that owns its own NADCAP/AS9100/ASME approvals and qualified-process library and publishes design rules plus an AI design checker, so abundant small hardware teams (energy, defence, robotics) can design to it. It owns the qualification, the capacity and the yield data, which compound per pour. It attacks castings and forgings lead times of 6-18+ months and the US having one foundry for certain large defence titanium castings. AI lever: captured foundry craft and solidification modelling cut scrap and training time, so one qualification serves thousands of customers' designs.

RETIRING-SHOP ROLL-UP WITH CRAFT CAPTURE: buy ASME/AS9100/NADCAP-stamped welding, machining and heat-treat shops whose owners have no successor (the 1.9M-unfilled-jobs cohort). Instrument the masters before they leave, train AI on their process, and move the shop's existing stamps and PQRs onto AI-coached novice crews (Hadrian-style 60-90 day ramps). This escapes the gatekeeper law because it buys stamps that already exist instead of queueing for new ones. On the law that sellers price in hope, target shops below PE size where succession, not growth, sets the price, a plausibility bet. It owns the approvals, the customer qualifications and the craft dataset.

RESURRECTION FLEET, generalised: own aging capital assets that are scarce because the craft to sustain them is dying, such as the 988 US peaker turbines 30+ years old (45.5 GW) bought at about $83-110/kW against $790-1,800/kW new. Captured craft (overhaul know-how, reverse-engineered parts with commercial-grade dedication) lets a small crew run them, and the company sells firm power. It owns the fleet, the operating evidence and the parts library. This is the AWS shape: owner of the scarce runtime.

BE-YOUR-OWN-APPROVER PARTS HOUSE: buy or build an FAA ODA/PMA holder or a 10 CFR 21 / commercial-grade dedication entity and use AI to industrialise the evidence package for out-of-production parts in aviation, nuclear and grid. Abundant AI-designed replacement parts become valuable only through the approval the company owns. Paperwork drops to near-zero marginal cost while the stamp stays scarce, which matches the law that AI fixes paperwork but not queues.

AI-NATIVE GRID-HARDWARE FACTORY THAT KEEPS THE FLEET: build standardised, hard-to-make, craft-limited grid equipment (large transformers, switchgear, modular substations) with captured winding and assembly craft. Keep ownership as a leased or rented fleet instead of selling units, so the company owns the installed base, the service agreements and the operating history. The factory is the internal compiler; the fleet and its evidence are the moat (the Intel/Microsoft installed-base shape, plus the Ford plant).

why_software_became_abundant: Four things, each cheap and copyable. (1) The runtime cost almost nothing: PCs, then the cloud, which anyone could rent. (2) Iteration cost about $0, so a mistake was a recompile, which let millions of mediocre builders learn by trial. (3) Knowledge and building blocks copied for free (books, Stack Overflow, open source), so each builder started on top of everyone else's work. (4) No licence was needed to ship, because a bug rarely hurt anyone physically. AI coding adds a fifth: it copies expert judgement into novices (the +34% novice lift in NBER w31161). Builders went from millions to 47M+.

mechanism: How the software monopolies broke: a closed, dominant system had a narrow interface that everything else depended on (IBM's BIOS and bus, Unix's syscall API, the phone OS, the ARM/x86 ISA). Someone reverse-engineered or re-specified that interface. Phoenix did a clean-room BIOS: one team wrote specs from IBM's code, a second team that had never seen it wrote new code. The new interface was then offered cheaply to everyone: Phoenix licensed its BIOS to OEMs for about $290k, and Linux, Android/AOSP and RISC-V were free or open. The cost of becoming compatible fell from "be IBM" to "pay a licence fee", so dozens of entrants built to the interface and the monopoly turned into a commodity market. IBM's share of PC-compatibles went from about 76% in 1983 to about 26% in 1986. Three things made it work. (1) Compatibility could be checked cheaply: if the software runs, it is compatible. (2) Copying and distribution cost almost nothing, so one clean-room effort served every clone maker. (3) The law allowed it: clean-room copyright doctrine, interfaces treated as functional, and later Google v. Oracle. Value did not stay with the leveller. It moved to whoever owned the next scarce layer that the clones all had to use: Intel (the CPU), Microsoft (the OS), and later AWS, which runs Linux as a fleet. Red Hat earned about $3B a year and sold for $34B, a small fraction of what AWS and Intel/Microsoft made on the same commoditised base.
hardware_analogue: The hardware equivalent of IBM's BIOS is the OEM aftermarket lock: proprietary spare parts, repair data and diagnostic software, and the approvals and service agreements that make a non-OEM part legally usable. Examples are gas-turbine hot-section parts and long-term service agreements, aircraft spares, Deere's Service ADVISOR tool, printer cartridges, and the sole-source spares DLA buys for defence systems. The clone strategy is a form-fit-function-equivalent part or repair, built by reverse engineering and certified separately. There are working precedents. FAA PMA lets a non-OEM make an aircraft part under its own approval; HEICO launches PMA parts at about 70% of the OEM price, and the gap widens to 40-60% below OEM as OEMs raise prices. HEICO deliberately stays at or below about 30% share in each part so OEMs are not provoked into a price war. In gas turbines, independents (PSM, EthosEnergy, Chromalloy, Wood) have taken service share and OEMs now hold about 62%, down from 65-80% since the 1980s. Printer cartridges show the legal side: Impression Products v. Lexmark (2017) held that once a product is sold, patent rights in it are exhausted, so remanufacturing became legal. The layer after the monopoly breaks is not the clone part. It is (a) the approval and evidence holder, which certifies equivalence and carries the liability, and (b) the operator of the installed fleet, who decides which parts go in.
why_software_became_abundant: The marginal cost of a copy was zero, so one reverse-engineering effort could be spread over unlimited units and clone makers. Compatibility could be proven at runtime for free: boot it, run Lotus 1-2-3 or the test suite. That meant buyers did not need a third party to vouch for a clone. The interface was a small, discrete spec, such as a BIOS call table, POSIX or an ISA, so the whole interface could be written down. Failures were cheap and reversible: a crash, then a patch. Network effects then concentrated value in the shared layer: once many clones existed, the software everyone ran on them (DOS/Windows, Android with Play Services) and the common component they all needed (x86, Qualcomm, cloud fleets) became the new monopolies. Abundance at the clone layer and monopoly at the next layer up came together.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical reasons. The 'interface' of a hardware part is not a call table. It is geometry plus material, microstructure, coatings, heat treatment and failure behaviour under heat, stress and cycling. Much of that is not visible from the part itself: you cannot read the casting process or the alloy's grain direction off a turbine blade. Showing equivalence takes destructive testing and operating hours, and each unit costs real money. Legal reasons. The monopoly is held by permission, not by code. In aviation the FAA has to approve each PMA part, and approvals take months to years. DLA has 12-18 month qualification queues and sole-source drawing rights. In nuclear, Appendix B and commercial-grade dedication apply. Parts that are not approved can void insurance, warranties and LTSAs. Copyright on firmware and anti-circumvention rules (DMCA 1201) protect diagnostics; it took the FTC suing Deere in January 2025 to try to open Service ADVISOR. Economic reasons. One clean-room effort only covers one part number for one machine family, and fleets are long-tailed: thousands of part numbers, each selling a few hundred units a year. Engineering cost per part does not shrink with volume the way software does. Buyers are risk-averse because downtime or failure costs far more than the price difference on the part. OEMs bundle parts into service agreements and tie them to performance guarantees, so a clone part has to replace a contract, not just a component.
what_ai_changes_now: As of 2026 AI does several things. It collapses the per-part engineering labour of reverse engineering. CT and 3D scans go to CAD; ML infers material and process from metallography and spectroscopy; physics-informed surrogates speed up FEA, CFD and creep/fatigue prediction; and drafting a technical data package, test plan and substantiation report falls from weeks of DER/engineer time to days. That changes the long-tail economics. A team that once could afford 50 part numbers a year might do 500 to 5,000, so the market a clone maker can cover grows by about 10-100x. AI also reads the OEM's own documents at scale (manuals, service bulletins, failure databases, obsolescence notices) to rank which parts to clone first by price gap and volume. It can run fleet condition monitoring, which builds the operating-evidence record. It makes compatible diagnostic and firmware layers far cheaper to build, the Phoenix-BIOS move applied to controllers. And with additive manufacturing plus AI process control, short runs of castings become viable. What it does not change: regulators still review in human queues (the FAA does not yet accept AI-generated digital substantiation in place of tests). Evidence still needs physical test hours and field hours. Foundry and casting capacity for single-crystal superalloys is still scarce. And incumbents get the same AI, so the OEM's cost to make its own parts also falls. On its own, knowledge stops being a moat for anyone.
where_the_analogy_breaks: (1) There is no zero-cost copy. Each clone unit carries material, process and test cost, so the leveller does not become a free standard like Linux; it is a 30-60% discount, not a 99% one. (2) Compatibility is probabilistic, not binary. A blade that fits and runs can still creep or crack at 20,000 hours, so it is never just "compatible": a trusted party must certify it and carry the liability. That party is the new gatekeeper, so the hardware analogue of the clone moment creates a new permission monopoly rather than abolishing one. (3) No single interface unlocks everything. IBM had one BIOS; GE has thousands of part numbers per frame. So the break happens part by part (HEICO's model), not in one Compaq moment. (4) There is little network effect at the part level. Owning more compatible parts does not create a Windows-style lock, so the new layer is held by evidence plus installed base rather than developer ecosystems. (5) Safety and liability law creates permission asymmetry by design, and it should: the optimism rule allows assuming the technology works, not assuming approvals arrive. (6) Open standards in hardware (RISC-V, OCP, Open RAN) worked where the product is a spec or IP block running on a foundry's process. The foundry (TSMC) and the integrators kept the value, which supports the point that scarce physical capacity is the real chokepoint.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says the leveller rarely captures most of the value. The PC: clone makers fought down to thin margins (Compaq was absorbed by HP), Phoenix stayed small, and Intel and Microsoft took the profit pool because every clone needed them. Linux: Red Hat made about $3B a year and sold for $34B, while AWS, Google and Azure capture far more by operating Linux fleets. The value went to the operator, not the distributor. Android: Google captured it through Play and services (about 70%+ OS share and tens of billions a year in Play revenue), and Qualcomm through the modem and SoC, while handset clones fought over thin margins. RISC-V: the ISA is free and value stays with the core/SoC vendors and TSMC. In the hardware aftermarket the pattern holds. HEICO (approval holder plus a large PMA library) compounded at roughly 20%+ a year for decades and became one of the most highly valued aerospace companies, while machine shops making the parts stayed commodities. Independent turbine service firms took share, but the asset owners and operators who buy cheaper parts keep the margin as firm-power profit. So the capture order is: (1) the operator of the installed fleet, who turns lower parts cost directly into margin on output such as power, flight hours or uptime; (2) the approval and evidence holder, because certification is the scarce layer clones can't commoditise; (3) holders of scarce physical capacity (casting, coating, test cells). The reverse-engineering or knowledge layer, the 'Phoenix' role, captures the least, and AI makes it even more of a commodity.
first_principle: When AI makes the cost of copying a hardware interface fall to near zero, the monopoly does not disappear. It moves to whoever owns the scarce layer that copying cannot reproduce: the approval, the operating evidence and the installed fleet. So the winner is the party that operates the asset and certifies its own compatible parts, never the party that only makes the clone. This is testable: in each case of a broken monopoly, the profit pool should end up concentrated in the fleet operator or approval holder, not in the reverse-engineering firm.
company_shapes: Resurrection fleet operator (the AWS move): buy old OEM-orphaned gas turbines (Frame 6B/7EA at about $83-110/kW against $790-1,800/kW new; 988 US peaker turbines over 30 years old, 45.5 GW), run them under your own maintenance programme, and fit an AI-built library of compatible parts and repairs. As both owner and operator you are your own approver: no LTSA, no OEM sign-off. You capture value as firm-power and capacity revenue, not as parts margin. mechanism:
Containers and virtualisation put one fixed interface (the OCI image plus the Linux kernel ABI, or the hypervisor's virtual machine) between a workload and the machine it runs on. That changed three things in software.

(1) Certification moved from the machine to the artifact. You test the image once and it behaves the same on any host that meets the interface, so "works on my machine" stopped being a problem.

(2) Moving a workload became almost free. The marginal cost of running it somewhere else fell to bandwidth plus seconds. VMs boot in minutes, containers in under a second. Datadog found the average container lifespan was 2.5 days against about 15 days for a VM (https://datadoghq.com/docker-adoption-2016), and adopters ran about 5x more containers by their tenth month.

(3) Capacity became fungible. Any compliant host can bid for any workload, which made utility compute (AWS, GCP) and bin-packing schedulers (Kubernetes) possible. Software became abundant because the expensive step, proving that this thing runs correctly here, was done once per artifact instead of once per site.
hardware_analogue:
The real analogue is not a CAD file or a "3D-print anywhere" marketplace. It is a qualified process recipe plus a verification envelope that travels with it: machine-independent parameters, material specification, in-situ sensor signatures and acceptance criteria. Any machine inside the envelope then produces a part that is legally and statistically the same part, and certification attaches to the recipe-plus-envelope rather than to the plant.

The one hardware industry that already did this is semiconductors. Mead and Conway's lambda-based, technology-independent design rules (1979-80) let a design be scaled across fab processes. MOSIS, from 1981, then gave universities fast-turn prototyping across shared fabs and is credited with starting the fabless industry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOSIS; https://ai.eecs.umich.edu/people/conway/Impact/Impact.html). TSMC (1987) made it a business: the PDK and design rules are the container interface, and any compliant GDSII "runs" on the fab (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundry_model).

Two other partial precedents exist:
- Aerospace is moving toward "part family" qualification in additive manufacturing, discussed at the FAA-AFRL workshop (https://www.nrc.gov/docs/ML1733/ML17338A886.pdf).
- ASTM work describes probabilistic qualification of alloy families that cuts cycle time 4-5x (https://store.astm.org/stp162020180137.html).

In both cases this is the move from certifying the plant to certifying the process.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today:
There are three reasons: physical, legal and economic.

PHYSICAL: there is no deterministic substrate. The same recipe on two machines of the same model can give different microstructure, porosity and residual stress. Laser calibration, gas flow, powder lot, humidity and fixture wear all matter. Bits copy exactly; atoms need fresh verification for every instance. NASA's additive standard (MSFC-STD-3716 / SPEC-3717, being replaced by NASA-STD-6030) ties a Qualified Metallurgical Process to a specific qualified machine. NASA's working assumption is that "changes to AM machines or aspects of the defined process nullify qualification and instigate need for re-qualification" (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20190002140/downloads/20190002140.pdf). Inspection alone was up to 25% of production time for GE additive engine parts (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150001636/downloads/20150001636.pdf).

LEGAL: approvals bind to an entity and a site, not to an artifact. Examples are FAA Production Certificates and PMA, NADCAP special-process accreditation per facility, ASME N-stamps per shop, DLA source-approval requests, and UL listings per factory with follow-up inspections. Liability follows the certificate holder, so the regulator wants one accountable plant.

ECONOMIC: process know-how is the incumbent's moat, unlike software, where the moat is the code. Tier-1 suppliers have every reason to keep recipes tacit and plant-specific. The buyer pays requalification per source, typically 6-18 months, which locks in sole sources. No neutral party owns the "kernel ABI" that would make recipes portable.
what_ai_changes_now:
What changes in 2026:

(a) In-situ monitoring with ML gives every build a high-dimensional signature (melt-pool, acoustic, thermal, spindle-load) and a per-part model of defect probability. Equivalence becomes a measurable, statistical claim: "this part's signature falls inside the qualified envelope." That is the container checksum for atoms.

(b) Physics-informed transfer models can map a recipe from machine A to machine B, or from powder lot X to lot Y, with a few calibration coupons instead of a full requalification campaign. The envelope becomes portable.

(c) Models can draft the qualification package itself: test plans, statistical allowables, FAI reports, traceability dossiers. The per-recipe cost of producing evidence falls sharply.

(d) Reverse engineering from scans, metallurgy and legacy drawings into a manufacturable recipe is now cheap. That builds the library of images to run.

What does NOT change:
- Gatekeeper queues. FAA, DLA, NRC and NADCAP still review by human cadence, and none accepts ML signatures in place of coupon or destructive tests today.
- The need for physical capacity: machines, furnaces, castings.
- Material supply.
- Liability concentrated on one certificate holder.

So AI collapses the cost of proving equivalence. It does not collapse the cost of being permitted to claim it. The only way around the queue is to be the approver yourself: operate the asset (owner-operator maintenance authority), hold the ODA/PMA, or do nuclear commercial-grade dedication in-house.
where_the_analogy_breaks:
1. Zero-copy versus per-instance verification. A container image is bit-identical everywhere. A hardware part is only statistically identical, and every unit carries its own evidence. Portability has a per-unit verification cost that never reaches zero, so software-style abundance becomes "cheap verification," not "free replication."

2. The host is not a commodity. Cloud hosts are interchangeable racks. Qualified machines are scarce, slow to build ($1-10M per cell, 6-24 months) and geographically fixed. The "anywhere" in "run anywhere" is bounded by capex.

3. Failure is not reversible. A bad deploy rolls back in seconds; a bad turbine blade or reactor valve kills people. Regulators will rationally lag the technology, and the safety control Dhruv requires lives exactly here.

4. There is no neutral kernel. Linux was an open, shared substrate. Hardware has no open "machine ABI." Each OEM (EOS, Trumpf, GE, Siemens) owns its controller, and some lock parameters.

5. Value lands in different places. In software, portability crushed the margins of the portable layer. In semiconductors, it concentrated value in the owner of scarce capacity: TSMC, about 70% of foundry share, $122.5B in 2025 sales (https://ocacnews.net/article/422076; https://www.guru3d.com/story/tsmc-captures-over-of-global-foundry-market-in-q2-2025).

6. Marketplaces stay thin. Xometry, the distributed-manufacturing network at scale, earned only 34.7% marketplace gross margin on $630M in 2025 revenue (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1657573/000119312526066959/xmtr-20251231.htm), because it routes jobs but owns neither the approval nor the capacity.
who_captures_value_when_it_works:
History says the portability layer itself rarely captures value. It goes to whoever owns the scarce thing above or below that layer.

Software:
- Docker Inc. created the container standard, gave the format to OCI and Kubernetes to CNCF, and sold its enterprise business to Mirantis in 2019. The leveller did not capture the value.
- AWS, Azure and GCP did, because they own the scarce capacity the portable workloads run on.
- Red Hat ($34B to IBM) captured the certified, supported, liability-bearing distribution.
- VMware is the exception: Broadcom paid about $69B because VMware owned a proprietary hypervisor installed base inside enterprises.
- The PC precedent points the same way: the clone-maker standard enriched Intel (scarce fab capacity and instruction-set IP) and Microsoft (the controlled interface), not the clone makers.

Semiconductors:
- MOSIS, the leveller, stayed a modest non-profit service.
- TSMC captured the capacity and the trusted process.
- Fabless designers who owned differentiated IP and demand (Nvidia, Apple) captured the rest.

Distributed manufacturing:
- Marketplaces such as Xometry and Protolabs' network capture a thin routing margin.

Lesson for hardware: when certified recipes become portable, value goes to (1) the owner of the certification and accountability, the Red Hat or TSMC-trust position, (2) the owner of scarce qualified capacity, the AWS or TSMC-fab position, and (3) the owner of the assets or demand that consume the parts. The recipe-sharing network or matching tool earns the least.
first_principle: When AI makes a hardware process portable (proving that a part made on any qualified machine is equivalent), the value moves away from whoever holds the know-how and toward whoever owns the certified recipe library, the qualified capacity that runs it, and the right to sign off on its output. So the winning company owns all three and sells the output, not the portability.

why_software_became_abundant: Software became abundant because portability made correctness something you prove once for the artifact, not once for every site. Three effects followed. Deployment moved from weeks of per-server provisioning to seconds. Capacity became interchangeable, so utility clouds could bin-pack workloads and sell compute at falling unit prices. And an open shared substrate (Linux, OCI, Kubernetes) meant nobody paid a tax to the interface, so millions of developers could ship to the same target. The pattern underneath: proving it works here was the gate, and once that proof cost zero at the margin, supply exploded.

mechanism: Software became abundant because a builder could ship without asking anyone first. Two things allowed that. (1) The law accepted that the builder owed the user almost nothing. Shrink-wrap and click-wrap EULAs that disclaim warranties and cap damages at the price paid were held enforceable (ProCD v. Zeidenberg, 7th Cir. 1996), and software was generally treated as a service rather than a product, so strict product liability did not apply. (2) The harm was mostly economic, it was spread thin, and it could be rolled back. A bad release cost minutes and a patch, not a life. CrowdStrike's July 2024 update shows how far this goes: Parametrix estimated about $5.4B of direct losses to the Fortune 500, of which only 10-20% ($0.54-1.08B) was insured, and the vendor's contractual exposure was capped near fees paid. With no outside gate, the release loop shrank to internal testing plus rollback, and Amazon was deploying every 11.6 seconds by 2011. Knowledge did not make software abundant. Moving the gate inside the company did: the builder decides alone when something is good enough, and the user (or nobody) carries what is left of the risk. The real principle underneath is that a gate exists wherever harm can reach someone outside the builder's ownership and balance sheet. Software's harm rarely did.
hardware_analogue: Hardware already has working ways to move the gate inside, and each has a track record. (a) Delegated authority: under FAA ODA, the FAA says it delegates about 94% of certain certification work, and GAO says more than 90% of certification work on new aircraft and parts is done by manufacturers. The FAA keeps final say: the certification basis, key decisions, and sign-off on each airworthiness certificate. (b) Self-certification by law: US cars have no pre-market approval. The maker self-certifies to FMVSS and answers afterwards through recalls and liability, which is why Waymo could deploy without a type certificate. (c) Owner-operator dedication: under 10 CFR Part 21 and RG 1.164 (Rev 1, April 2024), whoever performs commercial-grade dedication takes on the safety obligation, and utilities stepped into that role when vendors would not. (d) The insurer as gate: Hartford Steam Boiler (founded 1866) paired inspection with insurance, and its "Hartford Standards" became the industry's boiler specifications, the lineage that runs to the ASME code. UL began in 1894 with fire-underwriter money and $350 of equipment. (e) Owning the risk by owning the asset: Rolls-Royce's Power-by-the-Hour (1962) keeps the engine-health risk with the maker in exchange for flying-hour revenue, and services were more than half of a £11.3B group revenue in 2011. The true analogue is this: the gate moves inside the company when the builder is also the owner and operator, the only party seriously exposed, and the holder of an insurance-grade evidence record. In that position the builder approves itself, much as a software firm ships to its own servers.
why_hardware_lacks_it_today: Physical reason: hardware harm is kinetic, irreversible and often lands on third parties (bystanders, the grid, airspace). There is no rollback after a turbine disc bursts. Fleets share designs, so one defect is a common-mode failure, the CrowdStrike pattern made physical. Legal reason: strict product liability attaches to physical goods, and no EULA can waive wrongful-death claims by third parties. So the state requires evidence before the fact (type certificates, NRC licences, DLA and NAVAIR source approval), and delegation gets clawed back after failures. The 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people, the grounding and fixes cost Boeing about $20.6B, and the December 2020 act tightened ODA, with penalties for pressuring ODA staff and FAA sign-off on each MAX. Where the tail risk is catastrophic, the state socialises it: Price-Anderson pairs $500M of primary insurance per reactor with a pooled secondary layer of about $15B. Economic reason: trust is earned through slow, costly evidence (test campaigns, operating hours) that only incumbents have built up. Incumbents also own the parties who certify a part, the service agreements and the data rights. A newcomer cannot make the regulator or the insurer comfortable faster than the calendar allows.
what_ai_changes_now: What changes in 2026: (1) Evidence can be produced continuously and per unit instead of in occasional, expensive test campaigns. Fleet telemetry, physics-informed digital twins, CT and NDE scans read by vision models, and anomaly detection can turn every operating hour into an auditable safety record. The Swiss Re study of 25.3M Waymo miles (9 property-damage and 2 bodily-injury claims; 88% and 92% fewer than human baselines) shows operating data from an owned fleet can become the evidence that trust rests on. (2) The paperwork of being your own gate drops toward zero cost: AI can draft the FMEAs, Part 21 dedication packages, critical-characteristic plans, ODA procedure manuals, PMA test-and-computation dossiers, and audit trails, the work that made running an internal quality organisation expensive. (3) Underwriting becomes possible at small scale: an insurer that can read a fleet's live health data can price risk per asset and per hour. That revives the 1866 HSB model of inspection plus insurance without an army of inspectors. Parametric and captive structures let the operator hold the risk on its own balance sheet. What does not change: regulators still review at human speed and do not yet accept AI-generated or simulated evidence in place of physical qualification tests. Delegation such as ODA is granted to organisations with years of operating history and can be revoked. Third-party liability cannot be waived by contract. Catastrophic tails still need a balance sheet or a state backstop. And AI levels knowledge for incumbents too, so knowledge alone wins nothing.
where_the_analogy_breaks: (1) Rollback: software's real safety net was reversibility, and hardware has none. "Move fast" becomes "detect early and derate", which needs continuous sensing and margin, not speed. (2) Externalities: software pushed its residual risk onto users who accepted it in a contract. Hardware's residual risk falls on third parties who agreed to nothing, so the gate can come inside only where the asset sits behind a fence the operator controls: its own site, its own workers, a behind-the-meter power plant, a private range. It cannot come inside on public roads, in airspace, or for consumer products. (3) Correlation: an AI-generated parts library replicated across a fleet creates a common-mode failure, and one bad design kills many units at once. Insurers will cap this exposure, so the fleet needs design diversity or staged rollout, the hardware version of a canary release. (4) Backlash: delegated authority is politically fragile. One fatal failure under self-certification can end the right to self-certify for a whole industry, as the MAX did. (5) Scale economics: software's marginal copy is free, but a hardware unit still costs metal, so being your own gate removes the queue but not the bill of materials.
who_captures_value_when_it_works: History says value goes to whoever is accountable for the risk and owns the record of evidence, not to the party that levelled the knowledge. In software, Linux levelled the operating system. Red Hat captured value by selling accountability (certification, support SLAs, IP indemnity), essentially taking on Linux's liability, and IBM bought it for about $34B in 2019. AWS captured more by operating the machines itself and owning the uptime risk, so it never had to sell the code at all. In the PC, IBM levelled the architecture, and the value went to the two non-levelled bottlenecks, Intel and Microsoft, which kept their own rights to say what was compatible. In hardware, HSB and UL captured value by becoming the gate. Rolls-Royce and GE capture most engine lifetime value through service agreements in which they own the risk, not through selling engines. Boeing's ODA was worth billions because it turned the FAA's queue into Boeing's internal calendar. So when AI makes hardware knowledge free, value flows to (1) whoever owns the operating asset and sells its output, (2) whoever holds delegated approval or is the certifying body, and (3) whoever holds the loss and telemetry record that insurers price against. It does not flow to toolmakers or consultancies selling AI to incumbents.
first_principle: A gate stands wherever harm can cross an ownership boundary. So a hardware builder that owns and operates its assets, carries the risk on its own balance sheet, and publishes an evidence record an insurer will price becomes its own gate, and it then iterates at the speed of its evidence rather than its regulator. This is testable: in any sector, release-cycle time should fall as the share of output sold by owner-operators (rather than as products to third parties) rises.

The FAA says about 94% of certain certification work is delegated through ODA (79 holders), and GAO says more than 90% of certification work on new aircraft and parts is done by manufacturers: https://www.transportation.gov/testimony/faa-aviation-certification and https://avweb.com/flight-safety/faa-doesnt-do-most-aircraft-certification-work/

After the 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths), the 20-21 month grounding and fixes cost about $20.6B, and Congress tightened ODA in December 2020: https://kvia.com/news/business-technology/2020/03/10/the-cost-of-the-boeing-737-max-crisis-18-7-billion-and-counting/ and https://www.businesstraveller.com/news/congress-passes-faa-management-reform/

Price-Anderson requires $500M of primary nuclear liability insurance per large reactor (from 1 January 2024) plus a pooled secondary layer of about $15.0B across 95 reactors, the state socialising a catastrophic tail: https://www.morganlewis.com/blogs/upandatom/2023/09/large-increases-to-price-anderson-act-secondary-layer-protection-in-inflation-adjustments

Hartford Steam Boiler (founded 30 June 1866) combined inspection with insurance, and its 'Hartford Standards' became the industry's boiler specifications, an insurer acting as the gate: https://munichre.com/hsbeil/en/about-us/hsb-engineering-insurance/history.html and https://www.nationalboard.org/SiteDocuments/General%20Meeting/Brennan2019.pdf

UL began in 1894 with fire-underwriter funding, two employees and $350 of equipment, and later became the de facto US gate for electrical products: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UL_(safety_organization)

Swiss Re's study of 25.3M Waymo autonomous miles found 9 property-damage and 2 bodily-injury claims, 88% and 92% fewer than human baselines, showing an owned fleet's operating data can stand in for outside certification: https://waymo.com/blog/2024/12/new-swiss-re-study-waymo/

Rolls-Royce launched Power-by-the-Hour in 1962, keeping engine risk with the maker in return for flying-hour revenue; services were more than half of its £11.3B underlying revenue in 2011: https://www.rolls-royce.com/media/press-releases/yr-2012/121030-the-hour.aspx

NRC RG 1.164 Rev 1 (April 2024) on commercial-grade dedication: the entity that performs dedication takes on the Part 21 defect-reporting duties, and utilities took on dedication because vendors would not: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-04-29/html/2024-08963.htm and https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1995-09-19/pdf/95-23179.pdf
why_software_became_abundant: The law let the builder be the only gate. Enforceable EULAs (ProCD 1996) disclaimed warranties and capped damages at the purchase price, and software largely escaped strict product liability. The harm was economic, spread thin and reversible (rollback, patch). Insurance and the user absorbed the rest: on CrowdStrike, only 10-20% of $5.4B was insured, and almost nothing was recovered from the vendor. With no outside approver, the cost of a release fell from a shrink-wrap cycle of months to an 11.6-second deploy. Iteration speed then compounded quality: more releases meant more feedback, which meant better products, which let open source, cloud and SaaS spread everywhere. Abundance followed from free iteration, and free iteration followed from the builder being its own gate.
company_shapes: Resurrection fleet operator (the current best idea, now explained by this principle): buy old Frame 6B and aeroderivative peakers at about $83-110/kW, run them behind the meter or on the owner's own site for data centres and industry, and sell firm power, not turbines. Because the company owns and operates the units, it can dedicate its own AI-built replacement parts the way owner-operators do (RG 1.164-style), keep a fleet-wide telemetry record, and place the risk in a captive insurer that reinsures out to an HSB-style carrier. It owns the asset, the parts library and the loss record. The gate is internal because the only party exposed is the company, behind its own fence.

Owner-operated remanufactured grid equipment: own a fleet of AI-requalified large power transformers, breakers and switchgear (current new-unit lead times run to years) and lease them to utilities and data centres under performance guarantees, never selling the hardware. Run an in-house ISO 17025 test bay plus continuous dissolved-gas and partial-discharge monitoring, so each unit carries its own evidence. Value sits in the fleet and the operating record. The company holds the warranty the way Rolls-Royce holds engine risk.

Become the gate: acquire or build a recognised certifying body (an OSHA NRTL, an ISO 17025 lab, or an existing FAA ODA or PMA holder bought rather than applied for, which escapes the 6-18 month queue) and run it on AI-generated evidence dossiers. The company owns the permission itself, as UL and Boeing's ODA do, and owns a growing library of approved designs and parts it can then make or license. This shape fits the 'be your own approver' law directly.

Telemetry-native machinery insurer with an owned balance sheet: a modern Hartford Steam Boiler that insures only assets which stream health data to it, using AI to price per asset-hour, and whose inspection standards become the de facto spec for AI-built and remanufactured hardware. It owns the capital, the loss data and the standard. Builders who meet its bar get insured and financed, so it becomes the gate the market obeys before any regulator moves. It starts captive, attached to shape 1 or 2, then opens to others.

Defence and security hardware as a service from an owned fleet: own and operate counter-drone, perimeter-sensing or autonomous-logistics units on contracted sites (bases, critical infrastructure), selling outcomes per hour or per site rather than airframes. Operating them behind a controlled fence under the operator's own safety case keeps the gate internal, and the operating hours become the evidence for a later programme of record. The company owns the fleet, the operating hours and the data rights that incumbents normally keep.
